## Thesis

Social media has been neither simply good nor simply bad for democracy. It has strengthened democracy's capacity for contestation (exposing power, mobilising opposition, breaking official monopolies on information) while weakening its capacity for settlement (getting citizens to accept outcomes they lost). Where contestation is the scarce good, as under closed or semi-authoritarian regimes, the gains dominate. Where settlement is scarce, as in polarised established democracies, the costs dominate. Taiwan's experience suggests the imbalance comes from platform design, not from networked communication itself.

## Outline (about 1,500 words)

**I. Introduction: what democracy actually asks of citizens (about 175 words)**
- Open with Przeworski's definition: democracy is a system in which parties lose elections (*Democracy and the Market*, 1991). It needs people willing to challenge power, and also people willing to lose.
- Name the two functions: contestation and settlement. Note that "good or bad" debates usually measure only one of them.
- State the thesis.

**II. Contestation: what social media made cheaper (about 300 words)**
- Case: Belarus, August 2020. After the disputed election, the Telegram channel NEXTA became a main coordinating channel for mass protest under a regime that controlled broadcast media.
- Theory: Tufekci, *Twitter and Tear Gas* (2017). Networked movements can mobilise huge crowds fast, without years of organisation.
- Point: in this function, social media did what democrats hoped it would.

**III. The hidden limit inside the success (about 200 words)**
- Also from Tufekci: the movements that scale fast often lack the structures to negotiate, decide or turn a crowd into lasting power.
- Belarus again: the regime survived. Social media helped people contest the outcome but gave them no way to settle it.
- This links the two halves: the same features that speed up contestation fail at settlement.

**IV. Settlement: what social media made harder (about 300 words)**
- Case: Brazil, 8 January 2023. After Lula's 2022 victory, supporters of Bolsonaro who rejected the result stormed the Congress, Supreme Court and presidential palace. The protests were coordinated partly through messaging-app groups.
- Theory: losers' consent (Anderson et al., *Losers' Consent*, 2005). Democracies hold together when the losing side accepts the result, and closed groups that reinforce one side's story make that acceptance harder.
- Point: in an established democracy, contestation was already plentiful. What ran short was settlement.

**V. The deciding variable: which good is scarce (about 175 words)**
- Bring the cases together. The same tools strengthened democracy where contestation was blocked and strained it where settlement was fragile.
- This is the sharper answer to "good or bad?": the verdict depends on the country, and the essay can say which countries.

**VI. Design, not destiny: Taiwan (about 200 words)**
- Case: vTaiwan and the Pol.is platform, used in national consultations such as the 2015–16 debate on regulating Uber.
- Pol.is shows users the statements that win agreement across opposing groups, not the ones that drive the most engagement. This is a working example of networked tools built for settlement.
- Point: the imbalance follows from engagement-driven design choices, which suggests it can be changed.

**VII. Objection and reply (about 100 words)**
- Objection: Guess et al. (*Science*, 2023) found that switching Facebook and Instagram users to chronological feeds during the 2020 US election did not measurably reduce polarisation.
- Reply: a three-month change for individual users tests individual attitudes, not settlement at the level of a whole society. Concede that the causal link is still contested.

**VIII. Conclusion (about 50 words)**
- Social media gave democracies a louder voice for objection without a matching tool for agreement.
- The better question is not whether it has been good or bad, but whether it can be redesigned to help settle disputes as well as start them.

## Thesis

Social media has been good for democracy as participation and bad for it as governance. By making it dramatically easier for citizens to find one another and mobilize, it has expanded participatory democracy. But by bypassing linkage institutions and removing the friction Madison built into the extended republic, it has weakened the parties, organized groups and deliberation that turn public energy into durable policy and peaceful compromise.

## Outline (about 1,500 words)

**I. Introduction (about 175 words)**
- **Opening:** Social media is usually judged by what it lets people *do*, such as protest, post and organize. Democracy also has to *decide* and *govern*. Judging the platforms by mobilization alone captures only half the picture.
- **Definition of democracy:** Keep it broad, as you asked, and define it explicitly. One option from the AP Government curriculum is the three models:
  - Participatory democracy: broad citizen involvement.
  - Pluralist democracy: organized groups competing for influence.
  - Elite democracy: limited participation, with decisions filtered through representatives and institutions.
  - State that the essay judges social media against all three.
- **Thesis.**
- **Roadmap:** Three familiar cases, each reread to separate mobilization from governance.

**II. The participatory gain is real (about 225 words)**
- Social media lowers the cost of political action. Citizens can find like-minded people, coordinate quickly and reach a mass audience without money or institutional backing.
- By the participatory model's standard, this is a clear democratic good. More people can enter politics, and faster.
- **Federalist No. 10 link:** Madison argued that a large republic would make it harder for people with a shared grievance to "discover their own strength" and "act in unison." Social media removes that barrier almost entirely.
- **Pivot:** Whether that is good or bad depends on what happens *after* people mobilize. The three cases test that.

**III. Case 1: Egypt, 2011, reread (about 275 words)**
- **Standard reading:** The "Facebook revolution" shows social media empowering citizens against a dictator. Mubarak fell after eighteen days of protest.
- **Against the grain:** The networked youth movement that filled Tahrir Square did not win the elections that followed. The Muslim Brotherhood won the 2012 presidency. It had spent decades building offline organization, and the youth movement had not. The military removed President Morsi in 2013.
- **Mechanism:** Speed of mobilization stood in for organizational capacity. A movement that can gather a million people in days has not necessarily built the structures that negotiate, field candidates or govern.
- **Point for the thesis:** This is participatory success alongside a failure in what the pluralist model requires, which is organized, durable groups.

**IV. Case 2: The 2016 US election and Cambridge Analytica, reread (about 275 words)**
- **Standard reading:** Data-driven micro-targeting manipulated voters.
- **Against the grain:** The evidence that psychographic targeting changed votes is weak. The UK Information Commissioner's 2020 investigation found Cambridge Analytica's methods were largely standard and less powerful than the firm advertised. The deeper story is structural. Social media let candidates reach voters directly and build movements outside party control.
- **Mechanism:** Parties are *linkage institutions*, and one of their jobs is to screen candidates and build coalitions. Direct-to-voter platforms weaken that gatekeeping role.
- **Balance:** This cuts both ways. Weaker gatekeeping opens politics to outsiders, which is a participatory good. It also removes a filter that elite and pluralist models depend on.
- **Point for the thesis:** The harm is not mind control. It is that social media hollows out an institution that helps the system govern.

**V. Case 3: The 2020 racial justice protests, reread (about 250 words)**
- **Standard reading:** Social media spread video of George Floyd's killing and produced one of the largest protest movements in US history.
- **Against the grain:** The mobilization was enormous, but the federal legislative result was limited. The George Floyd Justice in Policing Act passed the House in 2021. Bipartisan Senate negotiations then collapsed, and no federal bill became law.
- **Mechanism:** Turning public pressure into a statute requires sustained interest-group work, coalition building and compromise in Congress. Those slow processes are the ones viral mobilization tends to skip.
- **Fairness:** Acknowledge real state and local policy changes, and note that the Senate's own rules mattered. This keeps the claim measured.

**VI. Counterargument and response (about 175 words)**
- **Counterargument:** Each failure has non-digital causes, including military power in Egypt, polarization in the US and the filibuster in the Senate. Social media is being blamed for problems it did not create.
- **Response:** Grant the point partly. Then narrow the claim: social media did not create these obstacles, but it shifted citizens' energy toward fast mobilization and away from building the organizations needed to overcome them.
- **Contrast:** The civil rights movement of the 1950s and 1960s relied on churches, the NAACP and years of slow organizing. It produced the Civil Rights Act of 1964.

**VII. Conclusion (about 125 words)**
- **Restate the thesis:** Social media is good for the first step of democracy and weak at the steps that follow.
- **Return to the definition:** Social media raises participatory democracy but weakens the pluralist and elite structures that translate participation into policy.
- **Closing line:** The question for American democracy is whether citizens can rebuild the organizations that social media lets them skip, not whether they can make their voices heard.

## Thesis

Social media has been neither simply good nor bad for American democracy. It has eased the Anti-Federalist fear in Brutus No. 1 that citizens of a large republic would be too distant to know or influence their representatives. But it has also undone the safeguard Madison counted on in Federalist No. 10: the difficulty factions face in coordinating across a large nation. The Arab Spring shows both effects at once. The same tools that let Egyptians bring down Hosni Mubarak in eighteen days could not build the institutions needed to hold power accountable afterward. Social media's effect on democracy therefore depends less on the platforms than on whether parties, courts, and a free press can channel the energy it releases.

## Outline (about 1,500 words)

**I. Introduction (~200 words)**
- Open with Egypt, January 2011. "We Are All Khaled Said," a Facebook page run by Google employee Wael Ghonim, helps call protesters to Tahrir Square. Mubarak resigns on February 11, after eighteen days.
- Turn: by July 2013 the military had removed Egypt's first elected president. Rapid mobilization did not produce a lasting democracy.
- Bridge to the U.S.: the Founders argued about exactly this trade-off between a people able to act together and a people able to deliberate.
- State the thesis.

**II. Brutus answered: social media closes the distance (~300 words)**
- Brutus No. 1: in a republic this large, people won't know their representatives, so they won't trust them or hold them responsible.
- Arab Spring evidence: ordinary citizens with no party or press access coordinated a national movement.
- U.S. parallel: citizens can reach officials directly, and campaigns raise money from small donors outside traditional party channels.
- Link to AP concepts: political participation and political efficacy rise when the cost of acting falls.
- Concede fully. This is a real democratic gain, not a side effect.

**III. Madison's safeguard removed: factions find each other (~300 words)**
- Federalist No. 10: in an extended republic it is "more difficult for all who feel it to discover their own strength, and to act in unison with each other." Size was the protection.
- Social media eliminates that difficulty for every group, whether or not its cause respects other citizens' rights.
- U.S. example: the "Stop the Steal" Facebook group, created after the 2020 election, gathered hundreds of thousands of members in about a day before Facebook removed it.
- Key point: the mechanism that helped Egyptian protesters is the same one Madison feared. The tool is neutral about which faction uses it.

**IV. Why both happen: mobilization without organization (~300 words)**
- Zeynep Tufekci, *Twitter and Tear Gas* (2017): digital tools let movements grow faster than they build the organizations, leadership, and decision-making that sustain them.
- Egypt 2011–2013: the protest coalition could topple a ruler but could not compete with the organized groups (the Muslim Brotherhood, then the military) that already had structure.
- U.S. parallel: linkage institutions such as parties, interest groups, and the press once filtered and organized public demands. Social media lets demands bypass them, which strengthens voice but weakens the step from voice to governing.
- This section carries the thesis. It explains why the same technology produces opposite outcomes.

**V. Rebuttal (~200 words)**
- Objection: polarization and distrust predate social media and have other causes, such as cable news, partisan sorting, and economic change. So social media is being blamed for trends it didn't start.
- Response: the thesis agrees. It doesn't claim social media caused democratic decline. It claims social media amplifies whatever institutions exist. That is why outcomes differ between a country with weak institutions (Egypt) and one with established ones (the U.S.).

**VI. Conclusion (~200 words)**
- Madison's remedy for faction was never to suppress it but to "control its effects" through institutions. Federalist No. 51's checks and balances apply the same idea.
- Restate: social media has handed citizens the power Brutus wanted them to have and stripped away the friction Madison relied on.
- Close by returning to Tahrir Square. The question is not whether people can gather. It is whether anything is built to hold what they gather for.

I used to put the staff rota out one week ahead. That was a mistake.

Now it goes out three weeks ahead. Last-minute sick calls have dropped from around six a month to two. Two people who had been talking about quitting are still here.

A week's notice looks reasonable from the manager's side. From the other side, it means you can't book an appointment, sort out childcare or make plans with anyone until a few days before. When people can't plan around their shifts, it's usually the shifts that give.

There are 18 people on my team, and every one of them has a life the rota has to fit around.

The lesson from my first year as a manager: before looking at how people turn up, look at how much notice they're given. This time, the fix was on my side.

Last-minute sick calls in my store went from about six a month to two this year. The change behind it was small: I started putting the rota out three weeks ahead instead of one.

I manage 18 people in a supermarket. A week's notice sounds fine until you're the one fitting a shift around childcare, a second job, a college timetable or an appointment you booked a month ago. With one week, when something clashes, calling in sick can be the only option left. With three, there's time to swap a shift or ask for a change.

Two people who had been talking about leaving also stayed.

That's the lesson from my first year as a manager I'd pass on. If you run a team on shifts, try putting the rota out earlier and see what happens to your numbers.

- **Counterargument:** Armies and economics caused these failures, not social media.
- **Response:** Social media didn't cause the failures, but it shaped the kind of movement that formed: fast, broad and loosely organized, which made it easier to defeat.
- **Taiwan:** The vTaiwan project used online tools to help citizens and officials reach agreement on issues like Uber regulation. That shows the tools can strengthen machinery when they are designed and used for it.

**VI. Conclusion (~175 words)**
- **Restate:** Social media amplifies voice, and institutions decide what that voice becomes.
- **Return to the hook:** Egypt had the voice in 2011 but lacked the machinery to keep what it won.
- **Takeaway for an AP Gov reader:** Democracies that keep strong linkage institutions can absorb social media's energy, and weak ones get overwhelmed by it.

## Thesis

Social media has been good for democracy as participation and bad for it as governance. By making it dramatically easier for citizens to find one another and mobilize, it has expanded participatory democracy. But by bypassing linkage institutions and removing the friction Madison built into the extended republic, it has weakened the parties, organized groups and deliberation that turn public energy into durable policy and peaceful compromise.

## Outline (about 1,500 words)

**I. Introduction (about 175 words)**
- **Opening:** Social media is usually judged by what it lets people *do*, such as protest, post and organize. Democracy also has to *decide* and *govern*. Judging the platforms by mobilization alone captures only half the picture.
- **Definition of democracy:** Keep it broad, as you asked, and define it explicitly. One option from the AP Government curriculum is the three models:
  - Participatory democracy: broad citizen involvement.
  - Pluralist democracy: organized groups competing for influence.
  - Elite democracy: limited participation, with decisions filtered through representatives and institutions.
  - State that the essay judges social media against all three.
- **Thesis.**
- **Roadmap:** Three familiar cases, each reread to separate mobilization from governance.

**II. The participatory gain is real (about 225 words)**
- Social media lowers the cost of political action. Citizens can find like-minded people, coordinate quickly and reach a mass audience without money or institutional backing.
- By the participatory model's standard, this is a clear democratic good. More people can enter politics, and faster.
- **Federalist No. 10 link:** Madison argued that a large republic would make it harder for people with a shared grievance to "discover their own strength" and "act in unison." Social media removes that barrier almost entirely.
- **Pivot:** Whether that is good or bad depends on what happens *after* people mobilize. The three cases test that.

**III. Case 1: Egypt, 2011, reread (about 275 words)**
- **Standard reading:** The "Facebook revolution" shows social media empowering citizens against a dictator. Mubarak fell after eighteen days of protest.
- **Against the grain:** The networked youth movement that filled Tahrir Square did not win the elections that followed. The Muslim Brotherhood won the 2012 presidency. It had spent decades building offline organization, and the youth movement had not. The military removed President Morsi in 2013.
- **Mechanism:** Speed of mobilization stood in for organizational capacity. A movement that can gather a million people in days has not necessarily built the structures that negotiate, field candidates or govern.
- **Point for the thesis:** This is participatory success alongside a failure in what the pluralist model requires, which is organized, durable groups.

**IV. Case 2: The 2016 US election and Cambridge Analytica, reread (about 275 words)**
- **Standard reading:** Data-driven micro-targeting manipulated voters.
- **Against the grain:** The evidence that psychographic targeting changed votes is weak. The UK Information Commissioner's 2020 investigation found Cambridge Analytica's methods were largely standard and less powerful than the firm advertised. The deeper story is structural. Social media let candidates reach voters directly and build movements outside party control.
- **Mechanism:** Parties are *linkage institutions*, and one of their jobs is to screen candidates and build coalitions. Direct-to-voter platforms weaken that gatekeeping role.
- **Balance:** This cuts both ways. Weaker gatekeeping opens politics to outsiders, which is a participatory good. It also removes a filter that elite and pluralist models depend on.
- **Point for the thesis:** The harm is not mind control. It is that social media hollows out an institution that helps the system govern.

**V. Case 3: The 2020 racial justice protests, reread (about 250 words)**
- **Standard reading:** Social media spread video of George Floyd's killing and produced one of the largest protest movements in US history.
- **Against the grain:** The mobilization was enormous, but the federal legislative result was limited. The George Floyd Justice in Policing Act passed the House in 2021. Bipartisan Senate negotiations then collapsed, and no federal bill became law.
- **Mechanism:** Turning public pressure into a statute requires sustained interest-group work, coalition building and compromise in Congress. Those slow processes are the ones viral mobilization tends to skip.
- **Fairness:** Acknowledge real state and local policy changes, and note that the Senate's own rules mattered. This keeps the claim measured.

**VI. Counterargument and response (about 175 words)**
- **Counterargument:** Each failure has non-digital causes, including military power in Egypt, polarization in the US and the filibuster in the Senate. Social media is being blamed for problems it did not create.
- **Response:** Grant the point partly. Then narrow the claim: social media did not create these obstacles, but it shifted citizens' energy toward fast mobilization and away from building the organizations needed to overcome them.
- **Contrast:** The civil rights movement of the 1950s and 1960s relied on churches, the NAACP and years of slow organizing. It produced the Civil Rights Act of 1964.

**VII. Conclusion (about 125 words)**
- **Restate the thesis:** Social media is good for the first step of democracy and weak at the steps that follow.
- **Return to the definition:** Social media raises participatory democracy but weakens the pluralist and elite structures that translate participation into policy.
- **Closing line:** The question for American democracy is whether citizens can rebuild the organizations that social media lets them skip, not whether they can make their voices heard.

## Thesis

Asking whether social media has been good or bad for democracy treats very different technologies as one. Its democratic effects follow from design: public, algorithmically ranked feeds and private, encrypted messaging apps shape participation, information and accountability in different ways. India's 2018 WhatsApp lynchings, and the forwarding limit that followed, show that changing how information travels can reach harms that rules about content cannot.

## Outline (about 1,500 words)

**I. Introduction (~200)**
- Open with India in mid-2018. Child-kidnapping rumours forwarded on WhatsApp were linked to a series of mob killings. In July, WhatsApp responded by limiting forwards in India to five chats and labelling forwarded messages. It changed the product and removed no posts.
- Make the point: the company could not police content it could not read, so it changed the plumbing.
- State the thesis, then preview the three mechanisms.

**II. Two designs, not one "social media" (~200)**
- *Public feeds* (Facebook News Feed, X, YouTube) are one-to-many, ranked by algorithm, and visible to outsiders.
- *Private messaging* (WhatsApp, Telegram groups, Signal) is one-to-few. It is unranked, end-to-end encrypted, and spreads through forwarding among trusted contacts.
- Explain why the distinction matters for a "good or bad" verdict. Most famous evidence (Cambridge Analytica, feed experiments) concerns public feeds. Much political communication in India, Brazil and Indonesia runs through messaging.

**III. Mechanism 1: Participation (~250)**
- *Feeds:* visibility lets movements mobilise fast. Tufekci (2017) argues this speed can come without the organisational capacity that slower movements built, which makes them easier to scatter after the peak.
- *Messaging:* the cost of joining is low wherever cheap smartphones dominate. Groups map onto family, neighbourhood, caste and party networks, so political talk moves through existing social ties rather than among strangers.
- Claim: each design widens participation, but for different groups and with different durability.

**IV. Mechanism 2: Information (~300)**
- *Feeds:* the usual worry is algorithmic ranking. Note the complication: Guess et al. (2023, *Science*) switched some US users to chronological feeds during the 2020 election. Time on the platform fell, but polarisation did not change significantly. Ranking may matter less than often assumed.
- *Messaging:* there is no algorithm. Trust in the sender replaces the credibility of the source, and forwarding strips away where a message came from. Banaji & Bhat (2019) found that pre-existing prejudice shaped which rumours people believed and passed on in the Indian cases.
- Claim: the same false rumour behaves differently in each design. On a feed it is a ranking problem; in a chat it is a trust problem.

**V. Mechanism 3: Accountability (~300)**
- *Feeds:* public content can be seen by journalists, researchers, fact-checkers and moderators, however imperfectly.
- *Messaging:* encryption hides content from everyone, including the platform. This protects dissidents and journalists, but it means content regulation has nothing to act on.
- India as the test case:
  - WhatsApp's 2018 forward limit and labels were design changes that left encryption intact.
  - The government's alternative was the 2021 IT Rules' "traceability" requirement to identify a message's first originator. WhatsApp challenged it in the Delhi High Court as incompatible with encryption.
- Claim: for private messaging, the democratic choice is between design friction and weakening privacy. That trade-off doesn't exist for feeds in the same form.

**VI. Objection and reply (~150)**
- Objection: the violence had social roots, and de Freitas Melo et al. (2019) found that forward limits delay viral spread but do not prevent it.
- Reply: design does not create prejudice. It sets how fast and how far a rumour travels before anyone can respond, which in a mob situation can be decisive. The thesis is about which levers exist, not a claim that design alone explains outcomes.

**VII. Conclusion (~100)**
- Return to the question: "good or bad" has no single answer because there is no single technology.
- The better questions for scholars and regulators are which design, which mechanism, and which lever.

**Sources (five; you need three):**
- Banaji, S. & Bhat, R. (2019). *WhatsApp Vigilantes*. LSE Department of Media and Communications.
- de Freitas Melo, P. et al. (2019). "Can WhatsApp Counter Misinformation by Limiting Message Forwarding?" *Complex Networks and Their Applications VIII*.
- Guess, A. M. et al. (2023). "How Do Social Media Feed Algorithms Affect Attitudes and Behavior in an Election Campaign?" *Science* 381(6656).
- Tufekci, Z. (2017). *Twitter and Tear Gas*. Yale University Press.
- Arun, C. (2019). "On WhatsApp, Rumours, Lynchings, and the Indian Government." *Economic and Political Weekly* 54(6).

# Thesis

**Working thesis:**
Asking whether social media is "good" or "bad" for democracy is a category error, because democratic effects follow from specific architectural features rather than from "social media" as a whole. India's WhatsApp lynchings of 2017–18 show that harm arose from one particular combination: encrypted private messaging, frictionless one-tap forwarding, and closed groups of trusted contacts. Together these made rumours both highly persuasive and impossible to hold anyone accountable for. WhatsApp's July 2018 forwarding limit shows that the democratically preferable response is to add friction by design, rather than to restrict content or let the state trace message originators. Design friction slows harmful virality without giving the state a surveillance tool. However, it treats the speed of spread, not the underlying prejudice, so it is necessary but not sufficient.

**Shorter version, if you want something punchier:**
The democratic impact of social media depends on its architecture, and India's WhatsApp lynchings show that slowing how messages move is a better democratic remedy than policing what they say or tracing who said them.

---

# Outline (≈1,500 words)

## I. Introduction (~175 words)

**Hook:** On 1 July 2018 in Rainpada, Dhule district, Maharashtra, a mob killed five men after WhatsApp rumours warned of child kidnappers in the area. This was one of dozens of similar killings across India in 2017–18 (e.g., Karbi Anglong, Assam, June 2018; Bidar, Karnataka, July 2018).

**Move:** Most debate asks whether platforms like this are good or bad for democracy. That framing hides the more useful question: *which design features* produce which democratic effects?

**Thesis:** As above.

**Roadmap:** (1) a framework for treating design as regulation; (2) how WhatsApp's architecture turned rumour into violence; (3) why the forwarding limit beats the alternatives; (4) the strongest objection, that prejudice rather than design is the real cause.

## II. Framework: Architecture as Regulation (~200 words)

**Topic sentence:** To see why the good-or-bad framing fails, we need to treat platform design as a form of governance in its own right.

**Evidence and points:**
- **Lessig, *Code and Other Laws of Cyberspace* (1999)/*Code 2.0* (2006):** behaviour is regulated by four forces: law, norms, markets, and architecture ("code is law"). The forwarding limit is a clear case of regulation through architecture.
- **Distinguish two models of communication:**
  - *Public algorithmic feeds* (Facebook News Feed, X, YouTube): content is visible, so it can be moderated, fact-checked, and studied, but algorithms amplify it.
  - *Private encrypted messaging* (WhatsApp): content is invisible to the platform, so it cannot be moderated. It spreads through personal trust networks, not algorithms.
- **Key claim:** These two models produce different risks and therefore need different remedies. You can't moderate content you can't see, so with WhatsApp the only available lever is design.

## III. How WhatsApp's Architecture Produced the Lynchings (~325 words)

**Topic sentence:** The lynchings were not simply "misinformation online." They resulted from three design features that, combined, made rumours credible, fast, and untraceable.

**Feature 1: Trusted, closed networks.**
- Messages arrive from family, caste, village, and neighbourhood groups, not from strangers. Trust in the sender carries over to the content.
- **Evidence:** Banaji & Bhat, *WhatsApp Vigilantes* (LSE, 2019): users trusted messages from people they knew and from ideologically aligned groups.
- **Optional additional evidence:** the BBC World Service study *Duty, Identity, Credibility* (Chakrabarti et al., 2018).

**Feature 2: Frictionless forwarding that strips context.**
- Before July 2018, a forwarded message looked the same as an original one. There was a quick-forward button beside media, and a message could go to up to 256 chats at once.
- Images and videos, often old or from other countries, travelled without any source information.
- **Evidence:** Garimella & Eckles, "Images and Misinformation in Political Groups: Evidence from WhatsApp in India," *HKS Misinformation Review* (2020): image-based misinformation was widespread in public political groups.

**Feature 3: Encryption makes content invisible.**
- End-to-end encryption means neither WhatsApp nor fact-checkers can see what is spreading until offline violence reveals it.

**Analytical point:** None of these features is harmful on its own. Encryption protects dissidents and journalists, and trusted networks support everyday civic life. *The harm came from their combination.* This is why "good vs. bad" is the wrong question.

## IV. Three Possible Responses, and Why Friction Wins (~375 words)

**Topic sentence:** The Indian case offered three possible responses (content removal, traceability, and design friction), and only friction addresses the harm without damaging democratic values.

**Option A: Content moderation/takedowns.**
- This is impossible on an encrypted platform without breaking encryption.
- The state's fallback has been internet shutdowns. India leads the world in shutdowns (Access Now's annual #KeepItOn reports). Shutdowns are a blunt tool that silence everyone, including people trying to debunk rumours.

**Option B: Traceability.**
- In July 2018, the Ministry of Electronics and IT pressed WhatsApp to act. Later, Rule 4(2) of the IT Rules, 2021 required large messaging platforms to identify the "first originator" of messages.
- WhatsApp challenged this in the Delhi High Court in 2021.
- **Argument:** Traceability gives the state a tool that would also expose government critics. In a context of democratic backsliding, this is a serious cost. It also targets the person who *created* a rumour, when the harm actually comes from thousands of people *forwarding* it.

**Option C: Design friction (WhatsApp's actual response).**
- July 2018: forwarding was limited to five chats in India, the quick-forward button beside media was removed, and a "Forwarded" label was introduced.
- January 2019: the five-chat limit was extended globally.
- April 2020: "highly forwarded" messages were limited to one chat at a time. WhatsApp reported a 70% drop in such messages.
- **Argument:** These changes are *content-neutral*. They apply to all messages equally, they don't require anyone to read messages, and they don't require identifying users. The "Forwarded" label restores some of the context that forwarding strips away.

**Concluding sentence for the section:** Friction is the only option that respects both free expression and privacy, which makes it the most democratically legitimate option.

## V. Counterargument and Rebuttal (~275 words)

**Counterargument 1 (the strongest): the cause is prejudice, not design.**
- Banaji & Bhat argue that misinformation spread because it confirmed existing communal, caste, and anti-outsider prejudices. Victims were often outsiders, migrants, or members of minority groups. On this view, focusing on design lets political actors off the hook.
- **Rebuttal:** Concede the core point. Design doesn't create prejudice. But design determines how *fast* prejudice can mobilise a crowd and how *far* it reaches. A rumour that takes days to spread gives police and local fact-checkers time to respond. This is why the thesis claims "necessary but not sufficient."
- **Supporting detail:** Offline interventions mattered too. Examples include the Supreme Court's guidelines in *Tehseen S. Poonawalla v. Union of India* (17 July 2018) and police awareness campaigns in Telangana's Jogulamba Gadwal district.

**Counterargument 2: friction doesn't actually work.**
- de Freitas Melo et al., "Can WhatsApp Counter Misinformation by Limiting Message Forwarding?" (Complex Networks, 2019): forwarding limits delay the spread of content but don't stop highly viral content from eventually reaching large audiences.
- **Rebuttal:** For lynchings, delay is exactly what matters. Violence happens within a short window of panic, so slowing the spread directly reduces the danger.

**Optional counterargument 3:** It is undemocratic for a private company, rather than an elected parliament, to make these decisions. You could briefly concede this, then argue that design standards could be *mandated* by law, which is a better role for the state than traceability.

## VI. Conclusion (~150 words)

- **Restate the thesis in new language:** The lynchings were a design problem amplifying a social problem.
- **Broaden the point:** The same analysis applies elsewhere. Researchers have studied WhatsApp misinformation during Brazil's 2018 election (Resende et al., 2019). Telegram has similar affordances. Public feeds need different remedies, such as changes to algorithmic ranking.
- **Final line:** Democracies should stop asking whether social media is good or bad, and start asking which design features they are willing to require.

---

# Recommended Sources (core five; you need three)

1. **Banaji, S. & Bhat, R. (2019).** *WhatsApp Vigilantes: An Exploration of Citizen Reception and Circulation of WhatsApp Misinformation Linked to Mob Violence in India.* LSE Department of Media and Communications. *Your most important empirical source, and also the strongest counterargument.*
2. **Lessig, L. (2006).** *Code: Version 2.0.* Basic Books. *Provides the theoretical framework.*
3. **Garimella, K. & Eckles, D. (2020).** "Images and Misinformation in Political Groups: Evidence from WhatsApp in India." *Harvard Kennedy School Misinformation Review.*
4. **de Freitas Melo, P., Vieira, C. C., Garimella, K., Vaz de Melo, P. O. S., & Benevenuto, F. (2019).** "Can WhatsApp Counter Misinformation by Limiting Message Forwarding?" *Complex Networks 2019.*
5. **Arun, C. (2019).** "On WhatsApp, Rumours, Lynchings, and the Indian Government." *Economic & Political Weekly*, 54(6). *Useful for the state-response and traceability section.*

**Primary sources:** WhatsApp blog posts announcing the forwarding changes (July 2018, January 2019, April 2020); the IT Rules 2021, Rule 4(2); *Tehseen S. Poonawalla v. Union of India* (2018).

Last-minute sick calls in my store went from about six a month to two this year. The change behind it was small: I started putting the rota out three weeks ahead instead of one.

I manage 18 people in a supermarket. A week's notice sounds fine until you're the one fitting a shift around childcare, a second job, a college timetable or an appointment you booked a month ago. With one week, when something clashes, calling in sick can be the only option left. With three, there's time to swap a shift or ask for a change.

Two people who had been talking about leaving also stayed.

That's the lesson from my first year as a manager I'd pass on. If you run a team on shifts, try putting the rota out earlier and see what happens to your numbers.
p2:
One year as a store manager. Here's the main thing I learned.

Management is mostly logistics, not inspiration.

I spent five years on the shop floor before I got promoted. I thought the rota was admin, something you knock out on a Thursday afternoon.

It isn't. For 18 people, the rota decides whether they can book a dentist appointment, sort out childcare, take a second job, or watch their kid play football on Saturday.

So I started putting it out three weeks ahead instead of one.

Last-minute sick calls went from about six a month to two. Two people who'd been thinking about leaving stayed.

No team-building day. No speech. Just a spreadsheet, finished earlier.

If you manage shift workers, the most motivating thing you can do isn't motivational. It's telling people when they're working far enough ahead that they can plan their lives around it.

## Thesis

Social media has been neither simply good nor simply bad for democracy. It has strengthened democracy's capacity for contestation (exposing power, mobilising opposition, breaking official monopolies on information) while weakening its capacity for settlement (getting citizens to accept outcomes they lost). Where contestation is the scarce good, as under closed or semi-authoritarian regimes, the gains dominate. Where settlement is scarce, as in polarised established democracies, the costs dominate. Taiwan's experience suggests the imbalance comes from platform design, not from networked communication itself.

## Outline (about 1,500 words)

**I. Introduction: what democracy actually asks of citizens (about 175 words)**
- Open with Przeworski's definition: democracy is a system in which parties lose elections (*Democracy and the Market*, 1991). It needs people willing to challenge power, and also people willing to lose.
- Name the two functions: contestation and settlement. Note that "good or bad" debates usually measure only one of them.
- State the thesis.

**II. Contestation: what social media made cheaper (about 300 words)**
- Case: Belarus, August 2020. After the disputed election, the Telegram channel NEXTA became a main coordinating channel for mass protest under a regime that controlled broadcast media.
- Theory: Tufekci, *Twitter and Tear Gas* (2017). Networked movements can mobilise huge crowds fast, without years of organisation.
- Point: in this function, social media did what democrats hoped it would.

**III. The hidden limit inside the success (about 200 words)**
- Also from Tufekci: the movements that scale fast often lack the structures to negotiate, decide or turn a crowd into lasting power.
- Belarus again: the regime survived. Social media helped people contest the outcome but gave them no way to settle it.
- This links the two halves: the same features that speed up contestation fail at settlement.

**IV. Settlement: what social media made harder (about 300 words)**
- Case: Brazil, 8 January 2023. After Lula's 2022 victory, supporters of Bolsonaro who rejected the result stormed the Congress, Supreme Court and presidential palace. The protests were coordinated partly through messaging-app groups.
- Theory: losers' consent (Anderson et al., *Losers' Consent*, 2005). Democracies hold together when the losing side accepts the result, and closed groups that reinforce one side's story make that acceptance harder.
- Point: in an established democracy, contestation was already plentiful. What ran short was settlement.

**V. The deciding variable: which good is scarce (about 175 words)**
- Bring the cases together. The same tools strengthened democracy where contestation was blocked and strained it where settlement was fragile.
- This is the sharper answer to "good or bad?": the verdict depends on the country, and the essay can say which countries.

**VI. Design, not destiny: Taiwan (about 200 words)**
- Case: vTaiwan and the Pol.is platform, used in national consultations such as the 2015–16 debate on regulating Uber.
- Pol.is shows users the statements that win agreement across opposing groups, not the ones that drive the most engagement. This is a working example of networked tools built for settlement.
- Point: the imbalance follows from engagement-driven design choices, which suggests it can be changed.

**VII. Objection and reply (about 100 words)**
- Objection: Guess et al. (*Science*, 2023) found that switching Facebook and Instagram users to chronological feeds during the 2020 US election did not measurably reduce polarisation.
- Reply: a three-month change for individual users tests individual attitudes, not settlement at the level of a whole society. Concede that the causal link is still contested.

**VIII. Conclusion (about 50 words)**
- Social media gave democracies a louder voice for objection without a matching tool for agreement.
- The better question is not whether it has been good or bad, but whether it can be redesigned to help settle disputes as well as start them.

## Thesis

Social media has made democracies better at contesting power and worse at settling disputes. It has widened who can expose and challenge those in office. At the same time, it has weakened the shared facts and trust that let citizens accept outcomes they lose. The real question is which of those two capacities a given democracy can least afford to lose.

## Outline (about 1,500 words)

**I. Introduction (about 175 words)**
- Open with Nigeria's #EndSARS protests in October 2020. Online mobilisation pushed the government to announce the disbanding of the SARS police unit within days. That is the contesting half.
- Then the Lekki tollgate shooting on 20 October. A Lagos judicial panel later found that soldiers shot unarmed protesters, and the federal government rejected its findings. Nigerians still don't share one account of that night. That is the settling half.
- Define the two capacities in a sentence each:
  - *Contestation:* the ability to challenge and expose power.
  - *Settlement:* the ability to reach decisions and accept results on shared facts.
- State the thesis.

**II. What social media strengthened: contesting power (about 375 words)**
- *Cheaper mobilisation.* Ukraine's Euromaidan began in November 2013 after journalist Mustafa Nayyem's Facebook post calling people to the square.
- *Exposure from below.* #EndSARS spread testimony of police abuse that had circulated for years without official response.
- *Evidence across countries.* Lorenz-Spreen et al. (2023) reviewed about 500 studies of digital media and democracy. They found consistent links to more political participation and information-seeking, with benefits clearest in emerging democracies.
- *The limit within the strength.* Tufekci (2017) argues that easy mobilisation skips the slow organising that builds lasting capacity. Movements can fill a square quickly and then stall. This prepares the turn to Section III.

**III. What social media weakened: settling disputes (about 450 words)**
- *Shared facts.*
  - In India in 2017–18, rumours about child kidnappers spread on WhatsApp and preceded a series of mob killings.
  - In July 2018, WhatsApp responded by capping forwards in India at five chats.
  - Forwarded messages in private groups leave no common public record that anyone can correct.
- *Accepting outcomes.*
  - Brazil's 2018 election saw mass WhatsApp campaigns, including reports by Folha de S.Paulo of businesses funding bulk messaging.
  - Romania's Constitutional Court annulled the first round of the 2024 presidential election after a TikTok-driven surge and intelligence reports of a coordinated campaign.
  - Key point: the annulment itself split the public. When the information environment is doubted, even the remedy cannot settle the dispute.
- *Trust.* The same Lorenz-Spreen review links digital media to falling trust, rising polarisation and populism, most clearly in established democracies.
- *Mechanism.* Keep this to one short paragraph: reach without a shared record, and ranking that rewards what spreads. Don't let this become the essay; the cases carry it.

**IV. Objections and responses (about 325 words)**
- *"Correlation, not causation; polarisation predates platforms."*
  - Grant the evidence limits.
  - Note that where a platform is the main news channel, as with WhatsApp in India and Brazil, the platforms themselves redesigned features in response to harms.
  - That doesn't prove causation, but it shows the people with the most data acted as if the link was real.
- *"Settlement isn't doomed: look at Taiwan."*
  - vTaiwan used the Pol.is platform to surface points of agreement in regulating Uber.
  - The government answered rumours quickly through its "humour over rumour" approach.
  - Concede this, then sharpen the thesis. Settlement suffers under platforms' default designs. Taiwan shows it can be rebuilt, but only by deliberate and often state-backed effort. So the claim is about defaults, not destiny.

**V. Conclusion (about 175 words)**
- Return to Lekki. The same tools that ended SARS have left the country without an agreed account of what happened at the tollgate.
- Restate the verdict: a democracy gets louder and better at refusing, but worse at agreeing.
- End on what follows for judging any one country. Ask which capacity it is short of, rather than asking whether social media is good or bad.

# Tideline: Basement Flood Early Warning for Apartment Buildings

## The idea

Tideline is a low-cost sensor network and alert system for apartment basements and parking garages. It doesn't just say "there's water." It measures **how fast the water is rising**, estimates **how long until cars are damaged**, and alerts **the right residents** in time to move their cars.

Your December 2023 flood is the pitch. The water rose overnight, nobody noticed, and 30 cars were damaged. Even a 30-minute warning would likely have saved most of them.

**Why it fits your judging criteria:**
- **Technical depth:** real hardware, signal smoothing, rate-of-rise prediction, rainfall forecast data, and alerts that escalate in stages.
- **Real-world impact:** a clear victim, a clear cost, and a clear fix. Each node costs roughly $15–30 in parts, compared with thousands per damaged car.
- **Continuable:** your own building is the first pilot site.

---

## What you'd build

### 1. Hardware (hardware person)
- **2–3 sensor nodes** placed at different points: the ramp entrance, the drain or sump, and the lowest parking bay.
- Arduino plus your water-level sensors. If you have an ESP32, use it for Wi-Fi. If not, send the readings over USB serial to a laptop acting as the "building gateway."
- **A local buzzer and LED on the node** that sounds even if the internet is down. Judges care about this kind of failure handling.
- **A physical model:** a clear plastic tub laid out as a mini parking garage, with numbered bays and toy cars.

*Note:* cheap resistive sensors corrode and only cover a few centimeters. They're fine for the demo, but mention that a real deployment would use waterproof ultrasonic sensors (e.g., JSN-SR04T).

### 2. Backend (you, Python)
- **FastAPI service** that receives readings and stores them in SQLite.
- **Prediction:** smooth the readings, then fit a linear regression over a sliding window to get the rise rate (cm/min). From that, calculate the **time until each danger level**:
  - ~10 cm: water at tire level (warning)
  - ~15 cm: exhaust pipes at risk
  - ~25–30 cm: water reaches door sills and floor electronics (critical)
- **Noise filtering:** require a sustained rise across several readings, and cross-check sensors against each other, so a mopped floor doesn't trigger an alarm.
- **Rainfall data:** pull the forecast from the free **Open-Meteo API** (no API key needed). If heavy rain is forecast, send a "pre-alert" before any water appears.
- **Staged alerts through a Telegram bot.** Telegram is free and instant, with no approval process like SMS.
  1. Building manager: "Water detected at ramp, rising 0.8 cm/min"
  2. Residents parked in affected bays: "Your car in B-12 is at risk in ~18 min"
  3. Everyone: critical alert
- **A "✅ I moved my car" button** in each alert, so the dashboard tracks which cars are still at risk.
- **Replay mode:** feed in recorded or synthetic sensor data. This is your backup if the hardware fails during the demo, and it also lets you replay a storm like December 2023.

### 3. Dashboard and brand (designer)
- A live **parking map** where bays shift from green to amber to red as water reaches them, and turn gray once the owner confirms the car is moved.
- A large level gauge, the rise rate, and a **countdown to critical**. This number is the emotional center of the demo.
- The Telegram alert copy. It should be calm, specific, and actionable.
- The pitch visuals: one slide on the 2023 flood and one on the path forward.
- Simplest tech choice: a plain HTML/JS page polling FastAPI, or Streamlit if the designer prefers to lay out components.

---

## 36-hour plan

| Hours | Hardware | Backend (you) | Designer |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0–3 | Wire sensors, get raw readings over serial | FastAPI skeleton, data model | Dashboard wireframes, name and brand |
| 3–10 | Calibrate readings to cm, build the tub model | Ingestion, smoothing, rise rate and countdown | Build the parking-map UI |
| 10–16 | Buzzer/LED local alarm, second node | Telegram bot, staged alerts, "moved" button | Wire the dashboard to the live API |
| 16–22 | **Sleep in shifts.** Don't skip this. | | |
| 22–28 | Make it rugged: mounting, tidy cables | Open-Meteo pre-alert, replay mode, noise filtering | Alert copy, pitch slides |
| 28–32 | **Full end-to-end runs with real water**, 5+ times | Fix bugs found in runs | Polish |
| 32–35 | Record the backup demo video, rehearse the pitch 5+ times | | |
| 35–36 | Buffer. Stop coding. | | |

**Cut order if behind:** rainfall pre-alert, then second node, then the "moved" button. Never cut the countdown or the phone alert.

---

## 3-minute demo plan

**0:00–0:30 · The story** (whoever tells it best)
> "December 2023. Our building's basement flooded overnight. By morning, 30 cars were ruined. The water didn't rise in an instant. It took hours. Nobody knew."

**0:30–0:50 · The setup**
Show the tub garage, the sensor nodes, and the live dashboard (all green). Say once that the demo runs on **compressed time**: real floods rise over hours, so the thresholds are scaled. Judges respect that honesty.

**0:50–2:00 · The live moment**
- Slowly pour water into the tub, or use a small pump for a steadier rise.
- The dashboard updates live: level rising, rate shown, **"Critical in 3:40"** counting down.
- Phones buzz. Hold one up, or project it: *"Your car in B-12 is at risk in ~3 min."*
- A teammate taps **"I moved my car."** That bay turns gray on the map.
- Optional but memorable: put a QR code on screen so judges can join the Telegram alert channel and get the alert on their own phones. Only do this if it worked smoothly in rehearsal.
- Briefly unplug the network: **the buzzer still sounds.** "It works even when the Wi-Fi doesn't."

**2:00–2:20 · The technical depth**
One quick slide or verbal summary: rise-rate prediction, noise filtering, rainfall pre-alerts from forecasts, staged alerts.

**2:20–3:00 · Impact and what's next**
> "About $25 per node, compared with thousands per damaged car. We're piloting it in our own building next month. After that: housing societies, then a shared street-level flood map built from every building on the network."

**Demo insurance:**
- Measure the exact pour amount and pour speed in rehearsal.
- Keep replay mode one keypress away if a sensor misbehaves.
- Have the backup video ready on a second laptop.
- Bring towels. Seriously.

---

## After the hackathon
1. **Pilot in your building.** You already know the failure point and the residents.
2. **Upgrade the hardware:** ultrasonic sensors, battery backup, LoRa radios for basements without Wi-Fi.
3. **Grow the network:** each building adds data to a shared neighborhood flood map, which becomes useful to cities and emergency services.
4. **Business paths:** subscriptions for housing societies, partnerships with insurers (who have a direct incentive to prevent claims), and integration with building management companies.

# Waterline: a flood watch for the car park nobody checks at night

## The idea

Around 30 cars were damaged because nobody noticed the water rising after midnight. Waterline is built for that gap between the water starting to rise and someone finding out.

A sensor in the basement pays attention to *rate*, not just level. When the water starts rising, it estimates how many minutes remain before it reaches the cars. It then calls people in order (a phone call, because a 1am text is easy to sleep through) until someone confirms they're on it.

Every alert is also a timestamped record of a basement taking on water, matched with the rainfall at that moment. That is the part for the engineer on your panel. A utility knows its pipes. It may not know which basements fill, or at what rainfall. Ask the engineer that question during your close.

## What you'd build

Five parts, one owner each. That matches a team of 3 to 5; double up if you're three. The sensor node needs someone comfortable wiring a microcontroller. If nobody has done it before, give it Friday night.

1. **Sensor node (hardware).** An ESP32 with a waterproof ultrasonic distance sensor (JSN-SR04T) mounted above the floor, plus a float switch as a backup that confirms there is really water. It publishes the water depth every few seconds over MQTT.
2. **Rise engine (backend).** This turns readings into decisions:
   - It smooths out noise.
   - It calculates the rate of rise.
   - It projects the time until the water reaches a depth the building sets, such as the bottom of the lowest car's doors.
   - It needs two signals to agree before alarming: ultrasonic plus float, or a sustained rise across several readings. This is your answer to the false-alarm objection, so make it visible in the demo.
3. **Forecast arming (data).** Pull rainfall forecasts from Open-Meteo, which is free and needs no key. When heavy rain is due overnight, the system moves into "watch" mode: more frequent readings and lower thresholds. On dry nights it stays quiet.
4. **Escalation (backend).** A Twilio voice call reads out the depth, the rate and the minutes left. It goes down a call list, building manager first, then residents, until someone presses 1 to acknowledge. A Telegram bot posts the same alert to the residents' group, so people know to move their cars.
5. **Two dashboards (frontend).**
   - **The building view:** a live depth chart, the projected time to the threshold, and who has acknowledged.
   - **The utility view:** a map showing basement flood events against rainfall intensity. Build it by replaying a synthetic multi-building dataset through the real pipeline, and label it "simulated" on screen. An engineer will respect the label and will distrust it if it's missing.

**Cut first if you run short:** the utility map, then the forecast arming. The sensor, the rise engine and the phone call are the product.

## Demo plan (3 minutes, live)

**The prop:** a clear plastic storage box as the basement, a few toy cars inside, and the sensor mounted on the lid. Put tape on the side of the box at your threshold. A small aquarium pump feeds water from a second container, so you control the rise and don't have to pour by hand. Rehearse the pump timing until the threshold falls about 90 seconds into the run.

| Time | What happens |
|---|---|
| 0:00–0:20 | No slides. "December 2023. Our apartment basement car park flooded overnight. Around 30 cars were damaged, because nobody noticed the water rising after midnight." Point at the box: "This is that car park." |
| 0:20–0:40 | Building dashboard. It is already in watch mode because of an overnight rain forecast (seed this so it's guaranteed). Say what armed it and why it stays quiet on dry nights. |
| 0:40–1:30 | Start the pump. The depth chart climbs live. Narrate the two-signal check as the float trips. The projection appears: "threshold in ~N minutes." |
| 1:30–2:00 | A teammate's phone on stage rings. Put it on speaker so the judges hear the call read out depth, rate and minutes left. The teammate doesn't answer, so the second phone rings. That phone presses 1. The Telegram group lights up with the acknowledgment. |
| 2:00–2:40 | Stop the pump. Switch to the utility view and replay the simulated multi-building data. Point out that events cluster at particular rainfall intensities. Name the design choice: every alert is a data point at basement level that the drainage network may not currently capture. |
| 2:40–3:00 | Close on the engineer. "Would basement-level flood timing be useful to your team, and what would it need to look like for you to use it?" That turns your last 20 seconds into a conversation with the judge most likely to care. |

**Demo safety:**
- Twilio trial accounts can only call verified numbers, so verify both stage phones on Friday.
- Have a local replay of a recorded sensor run ready in case Wi-Fi drops. The call can still fire from the replayed data.
- Bring towels.

# HangTime: will it dry today?

## The idea

A dryer is one of the most energy-hungry appliances in a home. People reach for it on doubtful days because they don't trust the sky. The worry is rarely "is it sunny." It's "will this be dry before it rains, or before I get home?"

HangTime gives one answer, not a weather report:

- **"Hang it out by 10:00, it'll be dry by 14:30."**
- **"Rain likely from 15:00: bring it in by 14:30."**
- **"Not today. Next good drying window: Tuesday morning."**

Drying depends less on sunshine than people think. It is driven by how dry the air is, by wind, and by warmth. A grey, breezy, low-humidity day can beat a still, muggy, sunny one. That gap between what people assume and what actually dries clothes is the insight your pitch rests on.

## What you'd build

The stack is a single-page web app, installable on a phone home screen as a progressive web app. It has no backend beyond static hosting, no accounts, and no hardware.

**Data:** the Open-Meteo forecast API, which is free and needs no key. You pull hourly values for your location:
- temperature
- relative humidity
- wind speed
- precipitation probability
- shortwave radiation
- vapour pressure deficit, a direct measure of how "thirsty" the air is

**The drying model:**
1. Each hour gets a drying rate from vapour pressure deficit and wind, plus a small bonus for sun.
2. You add hourly rates until a load counts as "dry." The user picks one of three load types (light cottons, mixed, towels and jeans), which sets the threshold.
3. The model looks for a window in daylight hours that finishes before any hour with high rain probability.
4. It outputs a hang-out time, a bring-in time, and a confidence level.

**The real data that makes it credible: a towel test.** Through the weekend, one teammate hangs a wet towel outside wherever they are and weighs it every 30 to 60 minutes on a kitchen scale. Wet weight minus dry weight is the water still in it. Log it next to the forecast for those hours and that location. This calibrates your model and gives you a measured drying curve to show judges. If it rains all weekend, the test still works: you recorded HangTime saying "not today" and being right.

**Two small features that close the loop:**
- **Bring-in reminder:** one tap adds a calendar event (`.ics` download) at the bring-in time. This is simpler and more reliable than web push for a weekend build.
- **Saved-runs counter:** the user enters their dryer's kWh per cycle once, from the energy label or manual. Each "I hung it out" tap adds a load to a running total of kWh and money not spent. All figures come from the user's own appliance, so no estimate is pulled from thin air.

## Build plan

**Kickoff (first few hours)**
- Fetch and render the hourly Open-Meteo data for the towel-test location.
- Hang the first towel and start the weigh-in log in a shared spreadsheet.
- Agree on the three answer screens: hang now, bring in by, not today.

**Day one**
- Write the drying-rate function and the window search. Tune the "dry" threshold against the towel log as data comes in.
- Build the main screen: one big answer and a simple timeline bar showing the hang-out time, the predicted dry time, and any rain.
- Add the load-type picker and browser geolocation.

**Day two, before demos**
- Add the calendar reminder and the saved-runs counter.
- Build the "why" view: forecast drying rate plotted against the measured towel curve.
- Cache a forecast JSON locally as a demo fallback, then rehearse twice.

Scope stop rule: if the model isn't calibrated by the end of day one, ship the window search on a simpler rule (no rain, humidity under a threshold, some wind). Show the towel data as "how we'll tune it next."

## Demo plan (about 3 minutes, story-led)

**0:00 The person.** Hold up a damp towel. Introduce one person with a load just out of the washer, a grey sky, and a dryer one button away. "This is the moment the dryer usually wins. Not because they don't care, but because they don't want to come home to wet washing."

**0:30 The answer.** Open HangTime on a phone, mirrored to the screen. The live forecast for where you're presenting shows one plain sentence: hang out by this time, dry by that time.

**1:00 Why you can trust it.** Switch to the "why" view. "We've been drying this towel since the hackathon started." Show predicted drying against the weighed curve, including any hours where the model was off. Being honest about the misses makes the rest believable.

**1:45 The rain case.** Pick a day in the forecast with rain coming. HangTime says "bring it in by 14:30." Tap the reminder and show the calendar event appear. This is the fear that keeps people on the dryer, handled.

**2:15 What it adds up to.** Show the saved-runs counter for the person's loads this weekend, in kWh and money, using their dryer's own label figure.

**2:40 Close on the person.** "They hung it out." Fold the towel, now dry or nearly so. End there, not on a market-size slide.

**Fallbacks:**
- If the connection drops, load the cached forecast.
- If the towel test went badly, show it anyway as calibration data. That is a stronger story than a perfect chart.

# Tip the Scale

**The idea.** A big animated balance scale on one web page. You pick two things you might choose between, such as a beef burger or a bean burrito, driving to the station or taking the bus, or a weekend flight or the train. You drop one on each pan and the scale tips, showing the kg of CO₂e on each side. Then you can stack a whole day on one side and see how far one swap moves it.

The app doesn't track anything, needs no account and asks for nothing to be logged. The point is that you'll remember which way the scale tipped next time you order lunch.

It suits your team because it's genuinely simple to build and genuinely fun to use, and the "cool" comes from the animation and the surprise, not from hard engineering.

## What you'd build

The whole thing is a static website with no server, no database and no login. That means nothing can break on demo day except the Wi-Fi, and even that can be handled (see below).

**Three pieces:**

1. **The data file.** This is a spreadsheet of 30 to 40 everyday items, exported to JSON. Each row has a name, an emoji, a category (food, travel, home, stuff) and kg CO₂e per serving, trip or use.
   - Food figures come from the Our World in Data food emissions charts, which are based on Poore & Nemecek (2018). Convert per-kg figures to a typical serving.
   - Travel figures come from the UK government's greenhouse gas conversion factors (per passenger-km). Pick a typical trip length for each item.
   - This piece needs no coding at all. Someone careful with a spreadsheet owns it.
2. **The scale.** This is one SVG or a few divs, with the beam rotated by CSS according to the ratio between the two pans. Cap the angle so huge gaps still look good, and add a little bounce when it settles. Show each pan's total in big type underneath.
3. **The picker.** This is a row of emoji cards by category that you tap or drag onto a pan. Add a "clear" button and a "load a day" button that fills one pan with a typical day's choices. That gives you a "swap one thing" moment: replace one card and watch the beam move.

**Scope by time** (you don't know the hours yet, so pick a level once you do):

| If you get… | Build |
|---|---|
| One evening | Two fixed dropdowns, the scale, and the numbers. Already demoable. |
| A full day | Emoji cards, the animation, 30+ items, and a mobile layout. |
| The whole weekend | "Load a day" mode, a share-image button ("I tipped the scale by 4 kg today"), and a sources page. |

**Tools:** Plain HTML/CSS/JavaScript, or React if someone already knows it. Host free on GitHub Pages, Netlify or Vercel. Anyone can learn the CSS rotation part in an hour.

**Splitting the work without knowing skills:** Divide it by job rather than by role. The jobs are the data spreadsheet, the scale and animation, the card picker, and the look plus the pitch. Whoever has never coded takes the data or the pitch, and both are essential.

## Demo plan

The demo works by letting the judges play rather than by walking through features.

1. **Before you speak,** put a big QR code on the screen that links to the live site. Judges open it on their phones.
2. **Start with a bet.** Pick a pair where the answer surprises people (your data person will know which ones). Ask the judges to guess which way it tips, then drop the cards on your screen and let the scale swing. Read out the real number it shows.
3. **Let them try one,** so for 30 seconds the judges drop their own pairs on their phones. That's the moment they remember: using it themselves, not watching you.
4. **Show a day.** Hit "load a day," swap one card, and show the beam move. Say the point in one line: you don't have to change everything, just know which choice is the heavy one.
5. **Point at the sources page** so the numbers have credibility. Close with what you'd add next, such as more items, local data for your country, or a browser extension that shows the scale on food delivery sites.

**Safety net:** Keep a local copy that runs offline on your laptop, and a 30-second screen recording of the scale tipping in case the projector or Wi-Fi fails.

**Subject:** Reducing fuel cost through route planning

Hello,

Fuel is one of the largest costs a fleet carries and one of the hardest to control. Prices move on their own. What an operations team can influence is how many miles each day's routes ask its vehicles to drive.

That is the problem our route-optimisation software addresses. It builds routes that cover the same stops in fewer miles and adjusts them when the day changes: a late order, a cancelled drop, a closed road. Fewer avoidable miles means less fuel bought for the same deliveries.

I would rather not quote a savings figure before understanding your operation, because the answer depends on your network, your fleet and how routes are planned today. A short conversation would let me learn that and tell you honestly whether there is a saving worth pursuing.

Would you be open to a 15-minute call in the next two weeks?

Kind regards,

p1:
A year ago, after seven years as a senior engineer, I became the manager of the team I used to be part of.

Four months in, one of my engineers resigned. In her exit interview, she said she had never received clear feedback from me.

I had genuinely thought things were fine. That was the problem. I'd mistaken the absence of hard conversations for the absence of problems. She deserved clarity, and I didn't give it to her.

So I changed how I run 1:1s. Every week now has a written agenda and a section called "one thing to change." It builds honest feedback into the routine, before small issues turn into resignations. No one has left since.

The second lesson took longer. For five months, I kept coding because it felt productive and familiar. Meanwhile, my code reviews piled up, and three releases slipped while the team waited on me. They didn't need another engineer. They needed someone to clear the path.

Letting go of the work I was good at felt like losing my value. In reality, it was the start of doing my actual job.

If you're an engineer stepping into management, learn these lessons sooner than I did. Your team pays for every month you wait.
p2:
In month four of my first year as a manager, one of my engineers resigned.

In her exit interview, she said she'd never received clear feedback on her work.

I'd thought everything was fine. That was the problem. "Fine" was my read of the situation, not something I had ever actually told her. It was a wake-up call.

So I started weekly 1:1s. Each one has a written agenda, and every agenda has a section called "one thing to change."

The written part matters. Without a set place for it, feedback tends to wait for a performance review or a crisis. With one, it's on the page every week, and neither person walks out assuming things are fine when nobody has said so.

Nobody else has left since.

If I keep one lesson from this year, it's this: people don't know where they stand just because nobody is complaining. You have to tell them, regularly, in a form you can both look back at.

Thank you to my team for being part of the year I learned that.
