In month four of my first year as a manager, one of my engineers resigned.

In her exit interview, she said she'd never received clear feedback on her work.

I'd thought everything was fine. That was the problem. "Fine" was my read of the situation, not something I had ever actually told her. It was a wake-up call.

So I started weekly 1:1s. Each one has a written agenda, and every agenda has a section called "one thing to change."

The written part matters. Without a set place for it, feedback tends to wait for a performance review or a crisis. With one, it's on the page every week, and neither person walks out assuming things are fine when nobody has said so.

Nobody else has left since.

If I keep one lesson from this year, it's this: people don't know where they stand just because nobody is complaining. You have to tell them, regularly, in a form you can both look back at.

Thank you to my team for being part of the year I learned that.
p2:
A year ago, after seven years as a senior engineer, I became the manager of the team I used to be part of.

Four months in, one of my engineers resigned. In her exit interview, she said she had never received clear feedback from me.

I had genuinely thought things were fine. That was the problem. I'd mistaken the absence of hard conversations for the absence of problems. She deserved clarity, and I didn't give it to her.

So I changed how I run 1:1s. Every week now has a written agenda and a section called "one thing to change." It builds honest feedback into the routine, before small issues turn into resignations. No one has left since.

The second lesson took longer. For five months, I kept coding because it felt productive and familiar. Meanwhile, my code reviews piled up, and three releases slipped while the team waited on me. They didn't need another engineer. They needed someone to clear the path.

Letting go of the work I was good at felt like losing my value. In reality, it was the start of doing my actual job.

If you're an engineer stepping into management, learn these lessons sooner than I did. Your team pays for every month you wait.

A year ago I became a marketing team lead, managing three people.

Most posts about a first year in management are built on hard lessons and rough patches. Mine was fine. I still learned a lot, and a fine year is worth writing about, because it's the year most new managers will actually have.

A few things worth knowing if you're leading a small team:

1. With three people, each one is a third of the team. One person's bad week is everyone's bad week, so you either notice it early or notice it late.

2. You'll probably still do some of the hands-on work. Decide which parts on purpose, or the calendar will decide for you.

3. A quiet year is not a sign nothing happened. Steady weeks where the work ships are the result, not the absence of one.

If you're about to step up: you don't need a dramatic story to know you're learning.
p2:
Twelve months leading a marketing team of three, and the most useful thing I can report is what I haven't mastered yet.

The core lesson is the one every new manager hears: your job is no longer the work. It's making the work possible for others. I agree with it completely. I just haven't finished learning it.

In marketing, that is harder than it sounds. The work is visible. A headline, a campaign brief, a launch email: every draft that crosses a manager's desk invites an edit, and every edit feels like help. On a team of three, the line between guiding and taking over is a single comment in the margin.

What the role asks for is mostly restraint. Asking what someone intended before suggesting what to change. Letting a strong version ship because it's theirs, even when it isn't the one you would have written. Judging a week by what the team moved forward, not by what you personally touched.

None of this is complicated. All of it runs against instinct, which is why one year isn't enough to get it right.

I'd rather say that plainly than wrap year one in a neat list of lessons. Management is a different job from the one most people are promoted for, and the first year is mostly learning how different it is.

Year two starts now. The principle stays the same. The practice is what I'm working on.

The most useful thing I changed in my first year as a supermarket store manager was putting the rota out three weeks ahead instead of one.

Last-minute sick calls went from around six a month to two. Two people on my team of 18 who'd been talking about quitting stayed.

It makes sense when you think about it. If you only know your shifts a week out, you can't book the dentist, sort childcare or say yes to a family thing. Something has to give, and often it's the shift.

There's a lot of talk about management as leadership, vision and culture. Mine has turned out to be mostly logistics. Get the boring things right, and people can actually plan their lives.

If you manage shift workers and want one thing to change, I'd start with how far ahead they know when they're working.
p2:
One year as a store manager. Here's the main thing I learned.

Management is mostly logistics, not inspiration.

I spent five years on the shop floor before I got promoted. I thought the rota was admin, something you knock out on a Thursday afternoon.

It isn't. For 18 people, the rota decides whether they can book a dentist appointment, sort out childcare, take a second job, or watch their kid play football on Saturday.

So I started putting it out three weeks ahead instead of one.

Last-minute sick calls went from about six a month to two. Two people who'd been thinking about leaving stayed.

No team-building day. No speech. Just a spreadsheet, finished earlier.

If you manage shift workers, the most motivating thing you can do isn't motivational. It's telling people when they're working far enough ahead that they can plan their lives around it.

- Zeynep Tufekci, *Twitter and Tear Gas* (2017): digital tools let movements grow faster than they build the organizations, leadership, and decision-making that sustain them.
- Egypt 2011–2013: the protest coalition could topple a ruler but could not compete with the organized groups (the Muslim Brotherhood, then the military) that already had structure.
- U.S. parallel: linkage institutions such as parties, interest groups, and the press once filtered and organized public demands. Social media lets demands bypass them, which strengthens voice but weakens the step from voice to governing.
- This section carries the thesis. It explains why the same technology produces opposite outcomes.

**V. Rebuttal (~200 words)**
- Objection: polarization and distrust predate social media and have other causes, such as cable news, partisan sorting, and economic change. So social media is being blamed for trends it didn't start.
- Response: the thesis agrees. It doesn't claim social media caused democratic decline. It claims social media amplifies whatever institutions exist. That is why outcomes differ between a country with weak institutions (Egypt) and one with established ones (the U.S.).

**VI. Conclusion (~200 words)**
- Madison's remedy for faction was never to suppress it but to "control its effects" through institutions. Federalist No. 51's checks and balances apply the same idea.
- Restate: social media has handed citizens the power Brutus wanted them to have and stripped away the friction Madison relied on.
- Close by returning to Tahrir Square. The question is not whether people can gather. It is whether anything is built to hold what they gather for.
p2:
## Thesis

Social media has been good for democracy as participation and bad for it as governance. By making it dramatically easier for citizens to find one another and mobilize, it has expanded participatory democracy. But by bypassing linkage institutions and removing the friction Madison built into the extended republic, it has weakened the parties, organized groups and deliberation that turn public energy into durable policy and peaceful compromise.

## Outline (about 1,500 words)

**I. Introduction (about 175 words)**
- **Opening:** Social media is usually judged by what it lets people *do*, such as protest, post and organize. Democracy also has to *decide* and *govern*. Judging the platforms by mobilization alone captures only half the picture.
- **Definition of democracy:** Keep it broad, as you asked, and define it explicitly. One option from the AP Government curriculum is the three models:
  - Participatory democracy: broad citizen involvement.
  - Pluralist democracy: organized groups competing for influence.
  - Elite democracy: limited participation, with decisions filtered through representatives and institutions.
  - State that the essay judges social media against all three.
- **Thesis.**
- **Roadmap:** Three familiar cases, each reread to separate mobilization from governance.

**II. The participatory gain is real (about 225 words)**
- Social media lowers the cost of political action. Citizens can find like-minded people, coordinate quickly and reach a mass audience without money or institutional backing.
- By the participatory model's standard, this is a clear democratic good. More people can enter politics, and faster.
- **Federalist No. 10 link:** Madison argued that a large republic would make it harder for people with a shared grievance to "discover their own strength" and "act in unison." Social media removes that barrier almost entirely.
- **Pivot:** Whether that is good or bad depends on what happens *after* people mobilize. The three cases test that.

**III. Case 1: Egypt, 2011, reread (about 275 words)**
- **Standard reading:** The "Facebook revolution" shows social media empowering citizens against a dictator. Mubarak fell after eighteen days of protest.
- **Against the grain:** The networked youth movement that filled Tahrir Square did not win the elections that followed. The Muslim Brotherhood won the 2012 presidency. It had spent decades building offline organization, and the youth movement had not. The military removed President Morsi in 2013.
- **Mechanism:** Speed of mobilization stood in for organizational capacity. A movement that can gather a million people in days has not necessarily built the structures that negotiate, field candidates or govern.
- **Point for the thesis:** This is participatory success alongside a failure in what the pluralist model requires, which is organized, durable groups.

**IV. Case 2: The 2016 US election and Cambridge Analytica, reread (about 275 words)**
- **Standard reading:** Data-driven micro-targeting manipulated voters.
- **Against the grain:** The evidence that psychographic targeting changed votes is weak. The UK Information Commissioner's 2020 investigation found Cambridge Analytica's methods were largely standard and less powerful than the firm advertised. The deeper story is structural. Social media let candidates reach voters directly and build movements outside party control.
- **Mechanism:** Parties are *linkage institutions*, and one of their jobs is to screen candidates and build coalitions. Direct-to-voter platforms weaken that gatekeeping role.
- **Balance:** This cuts both ways. Weaker gatekeeping opens politics to outsiders, which is a participatory good. It also removes a filter that elite and pluralist models depend on.
- **Point for the thesis:** The harm is not mind control. It is that social media hollows out an institution that helps the system govern.

**V. Case 3: The 2020 racial justice protests, reread (about 250 words)**
- **Standard reading:** Social media spread video of George Floyd's killing and produced one of the largest protest movements in US history.
- **Against the grain:** The mobilization was enormous, but the federal legislative result was limited. The George Floyd Justice in Policing Act passed the House in 2021. Bipartisan Senate negotiations then collapsed, and no federal bill became law.
- **Mechanism:** Turning public pressure into a statute requires sustained interest-group work, coalition building and compromise in Congress. Those slow processes are the ones viral mobilization tends to skip.
- **Fairness:** Acknowledge real state and local policy changes, and note that the Senate's own rules mattered. This keeps the claim measured.

**VI. Counterargument and response (about 175 words)**
- **Counterargument:** Each failure has non-digital causes, including military power in Egypt, polarization in the US and the filibuster in the Senate. Social media is being blamed for problems it did not create.
- **Response:** Grant the point partly. Then narrow the claim: social media did not create these obstacles, but it shifted citizens' energy toward fast mobilization and away from building the organizations needed to overcome them.
- **Contrast:** The civil rights movement of the 1950s and 1960s relied on churches, the NAACP and years of slow organizing. It produced the Civil Rights Act of 1964.

**VII. Conclusion (about 125 words)**
- **Restate the thesis:** Social media is good for the first step of democracy and weak at the steps that follow.
- **Return to the definition:** Social media raises participatory democracy but weakens the pluralist and elite structures that translate participation into policy.
- **Closing line:** The question for American democracy is whether citizens can rebuild the organizations that social media lets them skip, not whether they can make their voices heard.

A year ago I became a marketing team lead, managing three people.

Most posts about a first year in management are built on hard lessons and rough patches. Mine was fine. I still learned a lot, and a fine year is worth writing about, because it's the year most new managers will actually have.

A few things worth knowing if you're leading a small team:

1. With three people, each one is a third of the team. One person's bad week is everyone's bad week, so you either notice it early or notice it late.

2. You'll probably still do some of the hands-on work. Decide which parts on purpose, or the calendar will decide for you.

3. A quiet year is not a sign nothing happened. Steady weeks where the work ships are the result, not the absence of one.

If you're about to step up: you don't need a dramatic story to know you're learning.
p2:
A year ago I took on a marketing team of three. The most useful thing I've learned since fits in one sentence: my job is no longer the work. It's the people doing it.

That sounds obvious. In marketing, it is surprisingly easy to forget.

Marketers tend to be promoted for their craft: the sharp headline, the campaign that landed, the brief that rescued a launch. Those instincts don't switch off with a new title. When a draft arrives that isn't quite there, the quickest fix is to rewrite it yourself. It ships faster. It may even read better. And it teaches the person who wrote it only one thing: their version wasn't needed.

With a team of three, the arithmetic is unforgiving. Every hour spent redoing someone's work is an hour not spent making three people better at theirs. The leverage is no longer in the copy. It's in the feedback, the context and the trust that let someone own a piece from brief to launch.

That changes how a manager's week should be measured. "What did I produce?" is the wrong question. The right one is "What can my team do now that they couldn't before?"

That is harder to put on a dashboard. It is also the only measure that compounds.

One year in, here is the lesson I'd pass to anyone moving from doing the work to leading it: your craft earned you the role. Your team is the role.

# Idea: **GreenHour**: "Know the cleanest time to plug in"

**The pitch:** The electricity grid gets cleaner or dirtier through the day depending on how much wind and solar is running. Running your dishwasher at 2pm instead of 6pm can cut its emissions significantly, and it costs you nothing. GreenHour tells you **when** to run your energy-hungry appliances so they use the cleanest power.

**Why it fits your situation:**
- **Easy to demo:** You enter a location, pick an appliance, and get a clear answer like "Run it at 1:30pm and save 40% CO₂." Judges get it in 10 seconds.
- **Low technical risk:** One free API, no hardware, no machine learning, and no backend required.
- **Beginner-friendly:** Mostly frontend work, so mixed skill levels can all contribute.
- **Real and actionable:** It's not another carbon footprint calculator. It asks for no sacrifice, just better timing.

---

## What You'd Build

### Data source
- **[UK Carbon Intensity API](https://carbonintensity.org.uk)** is free, needs no API key, provides a 48-hour forecast, and works by region or postcode. This is the easiest option.
- If you're outside the UK, look at **Electricity Maps** or **WattTime**. Both have free tiers but require signup, so check coverage for your region first. Even if you're not in the UK, demoing with UK data is perfectly fine for a hackathon.

### Core features (must-have, about 24 hours)
1. **Location input:** a postcode or region dropdown.
2. **Appliance picker:** dishwasher, washing machine, dryer, EV charging, and so on, each with an estimated energy use and run time.
3. **Forecast chart:** carbon intensity over the next 24 to 48 hours, with the cleanest window highlighted in green.
4. **The answer card:** "Best time: 1:30pm. Saves ~0.3 kg CO₂ (42%) vs. running now."
5. **"Remind me" button:** downloads a calendar event (.ics file) or triggers a browser notification. Both are easy to build.

### Stretch features (if you have 48 hours or finish early)
- An impact tracker: "This month you've saved 4.2 kg CO₂, equal to X km not driven."
- A shareable result card for social media.
- A household or friends leaderboard.
- A "cleanest hour today" home-screen widget view.

### Suggested stack
- **Frontend:** plain HTML/JS or React/Next.js, whatever your team knows best.
- **Charts:** Chart.js (simple and well documented).
- **Hosting:** Vercel or Netlify (free, and deploys in minutes).
- **Backend:** none needed. Call the API directly from the browser.

### Rough team split (for 3 to 5 people)
| Role | Tasks |
|---|---|
| Data person | Fetch the API, find the best window, calculate savings |
| Frontend person | Layout, inputs, results card |
| Chart person | Forecast chart with the highlighted window |
| Design/pitch person | Name, logo, colors, appliance energy estimates, slides, demo script |

Whoever finishes first picks up stretch features.

### Timeline (24-hour version)
- **Hours 0–2:** Agree on scope, set up a repo, get one API call working.
- **Hours 2–10:** Build the core features in parallel.
- **Hours 10–14:** Connect everything and deploy a working version early.
- **Hours 14–20:** Polish the UI, fix bugs, add one stretch feature.
- **Hours 20–24:** Freeze features, rehearse the demo, record a backup video.

---

## Demo Plan (about 2–3 minutes, live)

**1. Hook (20 sec)**
> "Quick question: does it matter *when* you run your dishwasher? Most people think no. But the grid's carbon intensity can change a lot within a single day, depending on wind and sun."

Show one slide with a real carbon intensity curve from today.

**2. Live demo (90 sec)**
- Open the deployed app on a phone or laptop.
- Enter a postcode and select "Dishwasher."
- The chart appears with the green window highlighted. Point to it.
- Read the answer card aloud: "Run it at 1:30pm and save 42%."
- Tap "Remind me" to show the calendar event appear.
- If you built it, show the impact tracker: "Over a year, this one habit saves..."

**3. Impact (30 sec)**
> "No new appliances, no cost, no sacrifice. Just timing. If 10,000 households shifted two loads a week, that's [your calculated number] tonnes of CO₂ a year."

Work out this number beforehand and keep it conservative and clearly labeled as an estimate.

**4. Close (15 sec)**
> "GreenHour: the cleanest time to plug in." Then mention what you'd build next, like smart plug integration that automatically runs appliances at the best time.

### Protect against demo failure
- **Cache a copy of the API response** and add a fallback so the app still works if the Wi-Fi or API fails.
- **Record a 60-second screen video** of the full flow as a last-resort backup.
- **Rehearse at least three times** and time it.

# Born Hotter

## The idea

You type the town you grew up in and the year you were born. The page answers one question: how much hotter is that place now than when you were born?

It pulls real temperature records for that spot going back to 1940 and shows three things:

- One big number: the town's recent average year compared with the decade you were born in, for example "+1.4°C".
- A warming-stripes chart: one coloured bar per year from 1940 to now, blue for cool years and red for hot ones, with your birth year marked.
- A look forward: the projected temperature for that town in the year you turn 60, from climate model data.

Most climate apps ask you to log things, and beginners can't build a convincing footprint calculator in a weekend. This app asks for two inputs and gives an answer about a place the user cares about. Because everyone has a hometown, the demo is personal for every judge in the room.

## What you'd build

The whole thing is one web page with no backend, no database and no login. It uses three free Open-Meteo services that need no API key:

1. **Find the town.** The Open-Meteo geocoding API turns "Pune" or "Leeds" into latitude and longitude.
2. **Get the past.** The Open-Meteo historical weather API returns daily temperatures from 1940 to now for that point. Average them by year.
3. **Get the future.** The Open-Meteo climate API returns model projections for the same point up to 2050.
4. **Show it.** Display the big number, the stripes and the projection on one screen, using plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with Chart.js. A "Share my card" button saves the screen as an image.

Two design choices will make it trustworthy:

- **Compare decades, not single years.** One hot year can be a fluke. Comparing "the 1990s average" with "the last 10 years" is honest and still dramatic.
- **Say "around your town", not "your street".** The historical data is on a grid roughly 25 km across, so it describes the area, not one neighbourhood. Put that in one line at the bottom. Judges trust a team that states its limits.

**Splitting it among a few friends:**

- One person gets the API calls working and logs the numbers to the console. This is the riskiest part, so do it first.
- One person builds the page layout and the big-number card using fake numbers.
- One person builds the stripes chart.
- Whoever is free prepares the demo and the backup recording.

If all of that works by Saturday evening, everything else is a bonus. Possible stretch goals, in order:

1. The share card.
2. A "compare two towns" view for where you were born versus where you live now.
3. A line counting how many days last year were hotter than the hottest day in your birth year.

## Weekend plan

- **Friday night:** Everyone opens the three API links in a browser and confirms data comes back for one town. Pick names and colours. Stop there.
- **Saturday morning:** Get the APIs to produce a real big number for one hardcoded town.
- **Saturday afternoon:** Add the town and birth-year input and the stripes chart. Run the three-town test from above.
- **Saturday evening:** Add the projection and do styling. Save the full data for six or seven towns as files so the demo works without Wi-Fi.
- **Sunday morning:** Freeze features. Rehearse the demo three times and record the backup video.
- **Sunday afternoon:** Make only small fixes.

## Demo plan

The demo works by turning the judges into users.

**Before you start talking:** Ask one judge, "Where did you grow up, and roughly what year were you born?" Write it down. If they'd rather not say, use a teammate's hometown.

**Then:**

1. Say one sentence: "Everyone's heard the world is warming. We wanted to know how much it's warmed for you."
2. Type the judge's town and year live. Let the big number appear, then pause and say nothing for a second.
3. Point to the stripes chart and to the bar for their birth year. Show how the red increases toward the right.
4. Scroll to the projection: "And here's that town in the year you turn 60."
5. Run it on a very different town, such as somewhere much hotter or colder, to show it works everywhere and the pattern repeats.
6. Close with one line on why it matters. Abstract global averages are easy to ignore, but your own hometown is hard to ignore. Finish by pressing "Share my card".

If the judges' time limit is tight, skip step 5.

**Safety net:** If the live API is slow, switch to your cached towns ("let me show you one we prepared earlier"). If the laptop fails completely, play the recorded video.

# Gut Check: guess what matters, then see the real proportions

## The idea
Most people's sense of which climate actions matter is out of proportion. Small, visible habits feel big, and one or two large choices hide in the background. Gut Check asks four quick questions about your life, then gives you eight action cards to drag into the order you *think* matters most. Then it reveals the real order for you. The cards resize to true scale and reorder themselves, and the small habits shrink to slivers. At the end you get one move that matters for your life, plus a "gut vs. reality" gap score.

It has no logging, streaks or badges. It does its job in about 90 seconds.

## What you'd build
Everything runs in the browser. It needs no backend, no external API calls and no login, so nothing can break on stage.

**Screens**
1. **About you:** four inputs. These are weekly car km, return flights per year (short and long haul), diet (meat most days, some, none) and home heating type. A "load demo profile" button fills them instantly.
2. **Rank it:** eight cards to drag into your guessed order. Use a mix of high and low impact actions: recycle everything, switch to LED bulbs, wash clothes cold, skip one long-haul return flight, go car-free or switch to an EV, cut beef, move to a plant-based diet, switch to a heat pump or a green tariff.
3. **The reveal:** cards animate into the true order, and each bar's width is set by the kg CO₂e per year it saves *given your inputs*. Your guessed rank stays shown as a ghost position next to each card.
4. **Your one move:** your biggest lever in one sentence and your gap score. If an input zeroes an action out (you don't fly, so skipping a flight saves nothing), the card says so instead of showing a fake number.

**Data**
- A single `factors.json` file built from published sources. Use the UK government's greenhouse gas conversion factors (or the EPA's, if your judges are US-based) for car km, flights and heating. Use Our World in Data's food emissions figures for diet.
- Each action is one small formula in a `calculate.ts` file. Show the sources in a footer on the reveal screen.

**Stack:** React or Svelte, with dnd-kit or SortableJS for dragging and Framer Motion layout animations for the reveal. Deploy to Vercel or Netlify, and keep a local build ready for the demo.

## 24-hour plan
| Hours | Work |
|---|---|
| 0–2 | Pull the factors, write the formulas and sanity-check the outputs in a spreadsheet. Run the three-person test. |
| 2–5 | Input screen and demo-profile button |
| 5–9 | Drag-to-rank screen |
| 9–13 | Reveal animation, the part judges will remember, so give it the most time |
| 13–15 | One-move screen and gap score |
| 15–18 | Visual polish, projector-sized type, mobile layout |
| 18–20 | Sources footer and zero-value edge cases |
| 20–22 | Deploy, then test on a projector and on a phone |
| 22–24 | Rehearse three times, with the rest as buffer |

**Cut first if behind:** gap score, then mobile layout. Never cut the reveal.

## 3-minute demo
1. **0:00–0:20, ask the room.** "Which saves more in a year: recycling everything you use, or skipping one long-haul return flight?" Get a show of hands, and don't answer yet.
2. **0:20–0:45, about you.** Load the demo profile and change one input live, so judges can see it's real input.
3. **0:45–1:25, rank it.** Drag the cards into your honest gut order and say your reasoning out loud. The judges will be ranking along in their heads.
4. **1:25–2:10, the reveal.** Hit reveal and let the animation run in silence for two seconds. Then point at the slivers and at where your gut placed them. Answer the opening question.
5. **2:10–2:40, it's personal.** Set flights to zero and reveal again. The ranking reshuffles, which shows it isn't a fixed listicle. Read out the one-move sentence.
6. **2:40–3:00, close.** "Trackers make you log every coffee cup. This shows you the one or two choices that are bigger than all of them. It runs entirely in the browser on public conversion factors, and the sources are on screen."

**Demo safety:** run the local build so venue Wi-Fi can't hurt you. Because the whole demo is live clicks on a fast app, you don't need a backup video.

# Idea: **CleanHour**: "When should I plug in?"

**Pitch:** The grid's carbon intensity swings a lot during the day depending on how much wind, solar, and gas is running. CleanHour tells you **the cleanest time in the next 48 hours** to run your dishwasher, laundry, or EV charger, and shows how much CO₂ you save by waiting.

**Why it fits you:**
- **Frontend-heavy.** The core is a timeline chart and a clean UI, with no backend required.
- **Free, keyless data.** The [UK Carbon Intensity API](https://carbonintensity.org.uk) gives a 48-hour forecast in 30-minute slots, nationally or by postcode. You don't need credits or a dataset.
- **No LLM needed.** The core logic is simple math, so the demo can't be broken by an AI call.
- **Easy to explain.** Everyone understands "run it at 2am instead of 6pm."

*Not UK-focused?* Electricity Maps has a free tier with a signup key that covers many countries. Swap the data layer and keep everything else.

---

## What you'd build

**Core (must-have):**
1. **Location input:** a postcode, or "use national average."
2. **Appliance picker:** cards for dishwasher, washing machine, dryer, EV charge, and custom. Each has an editable default energy use and run time (e.g., dishwasher ~1.2 kWh over 2h, dryer ~3 kWh over 1.5h).
3. **48-hour carbon timeline:** an area chart color-graded green to red, with "now" marked and the **best window highlighted**.
4. **Recommendation card:** "Start at **01:30**. Saves **~410 g CO₂** vs. now (≈ X km of driving)."
5. **Add to calendar:** generate a `.ics` file entirely in the browser.

**Window logic:** slide a window the length of the run time across the forecast slots, average the intensity in each, and pick the minimum.
`saving = kWh × (intensity_now − intensity_best)`

**Polish (if time allows):**
- A "your week" tracker stored in `localStorage` that tallies total CO₂ saved, with a little streak or leaf badge.
- A "Why is it cleaner?" tooltip showing the generation mix (the API provides it).
- A shareable result card.

**Stretch (only if everything else is done):** a plain-English one-liner such as "Windy tonight, so the grid is cleanest after midnight." You can generate it from the mix data with templates, so you don't need an LLM.

**Stack:** React or Next.js with Vite, Recharts or Chart.js, and Tailwind. Deploy to Vercel or Netlify.

**Safety net:** save a snapshot of the API response as `fallback.json` early on. If the live call fails during the demo, the app loads the snapshot silently.

---

## 24-hour build plan

| Hours | Goal |
|---|---|
| 0–2 | Scaffold, fetch the API, log data, save `fallback.json` |
| 2–6 | Timeline chart with now marker and gradient |
| 6–9 | Appliance picker, window algorithm, recommendation card |
| 9–10 | **Deploy.** You now have a working MVP |
| 10–16 | Visual polish, mobile layout, loading and error states, `.ics` export |
| 16–19 | Savings tracker and generation-mix tooltip |
| 19–21 | Rehearse the demo and fix rough edges |
| 21–24 | Buffer and sleep. Don't add features now |

---

## 3-minute demo script

**0:00–0:30, the hook.** "The same load of laundry can have double the carbon footprint depending on *when* you run it. The grid changes every half hour, but nobody can see that. CleanHour makes it visible."

**0:30–1:45, the live flow.**
- Enter a postcode and the chart animates in. Point out the clean dip: "Look, the grid gets much greener overnight because of wind."
- Tap **Dishwasher**. The best window lights up: "Start at 1:30am, save 410g of CO₂."
- Switch to **EV charge** to show the bigger number: "That's like skipping a 20km drive."
- Click **Add to calendar** and show the event appear.

**1:45–2:30, the impact.** Open the tracker: "One user doing this for a month saves about ___ kg." Then scale it up: "If 10,000 households shifted just their dishwasher…" Calculate these figures beforehand.

**2:30–3:00, the close.** "It's free, uses open data, needs no smart home and no signup. Next steps: more countries, and smart-plug integration to schedule appliances automatically."

**Demo tips:** pre-load the tab, bookmark a postcode with an interesting curve, and know that `fallback.json` will cover you if the Wi-Fi dies.

Four months after I became a manager, one of my engineers left. In her exit interview she said she'd never received clear feedback on her work.

I genuinely thought things were fine.

I've now spent a year managing a team of six in hospital IT. Here are three things that year taught me.

Thinking things are fine isn't the same as saying so. It's easy to assume that if you're not raising problems, people know where they stand. They don't. When a manager says nothing, the team hears nothing, not approval.

A written format beats meaning well. After she left, I started weekly 1:1s with a written agenda and a section called "one thing to change." Feedback now has a fixed slot every week. Nobody else has left since. I can't prove that's the reason.

The work you were promoted for can become the work you're blocking. I kept coding for my first five months. My reviews ran late, and three releases slipped because of it. It's easy to hold on to the job you were good at. But a manager who is also the team's reviewer becomes a queue.

What links all three: my costliest mistakes this year weren't things I did. They were things I didn't do: feedback I didn't give, and reviews I didn't get to in time.
p2:
In month four, one of my engineers quit.

In her exit interview, she told me she'd never once had clear feedback on her work.

I'd thought things were fine.

It made me realise that being liked and being a good manager aren't necessarily the same thing.

A friendly working relationship can sit right on top of someone having no idea where they stand. When nobody complains, it's easy to read that as things going well. Sometimes it just means nobody has been told anything they could react to.

So I started weekly 1:1s with a written agenda and one thing to change.

The written part matters. "Good work" is easy to say and hard to act on. A named thing to change is something you can both come back to the following week. With one on the page, it's much harder for either person to leave the room assuming everything's fine.

If you manage people, don't wait for an exit interview to find out what they needed from you.

## Thesis

Debates over whether social media has been good or bad for democracy treat two different technologies as one. Algorithmic public feeds rank content by predicted engagement and so shape what citizens see. Encrypted messaging apps rank nothing; they move content through trusted personal networks that no platform, journalist or court can observe. India's 2018 WhatsApp lynchings show that the second architecture can produce deadly political harm with no algorithm involved. They also show that the most effective response was a design change to sharing mechanics, the limit on forwarding to five chats, rather than content moderation. Social media's democratic effects follow specific design features, so they must be judged, and governed, platform by platform.

## Outline (about 1,500 words)

**I. Introduction (about 200 words)**
- Open with the 2018 wave of killings in India. Rumours about child kidnappers spread through WhatsApp forwards, and mobs attacked strangers. The most cited example is Rainpada, Maharashtra, in July 2018, where five men were killed.
- WhatsApp's response that month was to limit forwarding to five chats in India, label forwarded messages, and remove the quick-forward button beside media.
- The problem: most of the "social media and democracy" debate is built on Facebook, Twitter and YouTube feeds, and the Indian case doesn't fit that model.
- State the thesis.

**II. Two architectures, two kinds of democratic risk (about 250 words)**
- *Public algorithmic feeds:* one-to-many broadcasting, ranked by predicted engagement, publicly visible, and moderated by the platform. Their democratic risk is distorted salience, meaning which issues, actors and emotions get amplified.
- *Private encrypted messaging:* many small groups, unranked, spread through personal trust, and invisible to the platform. Their democratic risk is unaccountable mobilization: rumours carry the credibility of the friend or relative who forwarded them, and no one outside can correct them.
- Conclude that the two architectures need different diagnostics and different remedies, and that the rest of the essay tests this claim.

**III. Case study: WhatsApp in India, 2018 (about 350 words)**
- How the rumours spread. Banaji and Bhat (2019) find that misinformation travelled through trusted groups and landed on existing prejudice against outsiders and minorities. Ranking played no part.
- Why feed-style fixes could not work. End-to-end encryption rules out downranking, content labels based on reading the message, and takedowns. The platform cannot see what is being said.
- The design response, all aimed at the mechanics of sharing rather than at content:
  - the five-chat forward limit and the "Forwarded" label in India (July 2018);
  - the five-chat limit applied globally (January 2019);
  - "frequently forwarded" messages limited to one chat (April 2020).
- What the limit did. De Freitas Melo et al. find that forwarding limits slow viral spread but do not stop it.
- Lesson: in messaging systems, friction is the main lever. That lever acts on speed, not on what people believe.

**IV. Contrast: what changing a feed does and doesn't do (about 300 words)**
- Huszár et al. (2022) show that Twitter's ranking algorithm amplified some political content more than a chronological timeline did. In feeds, design visibly shapes exposure.
- Guess et al. (2023) moved Facebook and Instagram users to chronological feeds during the 2020 US election. Exposure and time spent changed, but polarization did not measurably shift over three months.
- What this means for the thesis:
  - Feed harms sit in exposure and salience, so remedies are about ranking.
  - Messaging harms sit in velocity and trust, so remedies are about friction.
  - A single "social media" verdict misses both.

**V. Objection and response (about 250 words)**
- *Objection:* the lynchings were caused by communal tension, low institutional trust and political actors, not by an app. Design is downstream of society.
- *Response:* concede that design does not create grievances. Argue that it sets how fast and how far a grievance becomes action, and that this is the part of the problem a democracy can actually regulate.
- *Complication:* the Indian government's 2021 IT Rules demanded that platforms be able to trace a message to its originator, and WhatsApp challenged this in court as a threat to encryption. This shows that the wrong diagnosis can produce a remedy that itself harms democratic rights, here privacy and free expression. That strengthens the case for design-specific analysis.

**VI. Conclusion (about 150 words)**
- Replace "good or bad" with a set of design questions to ask of any platform:
  - Does it rank content?
  - Can outsiders see what spreads?
  - What does it cost a user to share?
- Restate the comparison: feeds need accountability for how they rank, and messaging apps need friction that does not break encryption.
- Close by returning to the 2018 forward limit. It was a small change to a single button, and it shows where democratic leverage over these platforms actually lies.

## Thesis

Asking whether social media has been good or bad for democracy treats two different architectures as one. On public algorithmic feeds, the harm runs through what the platform chooses to amplify, so ranking can be audited and changed. On private encrypted messaging, the harm runs through trusted personal networks that the platform cannot see, so the only design levers are friction and the only lasting remedies sit offline. India's WhatsApp lynchings, and the limited effect of the 2018 forwarding cap, show that democracies need to regulate social media mechanism by mechanism rather than issue a single verdict.

## Outline (about 1,500 words)

**I. Introduction (about 200 words)**
- Open with the July 2018 child-kidnapping rumours in India and the killing of five men in Rainpada, Dhule district, weeks before WhatsApp limited forwarding to five chats.
- Point out that no algorithm ranked those messages. They moved from phone to phone through family and community groups. A verdict built on "the algorithm" cannot explain this case.
- State the thesis, then preview the three mechanisms and the counterargument.

**II. Mechanism 1: Amplification on public algorithmic feeds (about 250 words)**
- On Facebook, YouTube, X and Instagram, reach is decided by the platform's ranking, so harm here is a matter of what gets amplified.
- Evidence that ranking shapes political exposure: Huszár et al. (2022) on algorithmic amplification of politics on Twitter.
- Complicate it with Guess et al. (2023). Switching users to chronological feeds changed what they saw but did not measurably reduce polarisation. Ranking matters, but it is not the whole story.
- Democratic point: because the content is public and the ranking can be audited, it can be governed by transparency rules, researcher access and changes to ranking.

**III. Mechanism 2: Trusted relay on private encrypted messaging (about 350 words; the core section)**
- How WhatsApp works: there is no feed or ranking. Messages spread by forwarding, and they borrow credibility from the person who sent them, a relative or neighbour rather than a stranger.
- India case: child-kidnapping rumours circulated as images, voice notes and video clips in local groups (Banaji & Bhat, 2019). Garimella & Eckles (2020) found that images carry much of the misinformation in Indian political WhatsApp groups.
- Why the feed-era toolkit fails here. End-to-end encryption means the platform cannot see, fact-check, label or down-rank content, and outside researchers cannot audit it.
- Democratic point: the same privacy that protects dissidents and journalists also lets rumours travel without anyone seeing them. The harm comes from the design, not from moderation failures.

**IV. Mechanism 3: Mechanisms determine remedies (about 300 words)**
- The July 2018 forwarding limit was friction, not content moderation. WhatsApp slowed sharing without reading messages.
- Its effect was limited. Melo et al. (2019) found that forwarding limits delay spread but do not stop viral content from reaching most of the network.
- The Indian state reached for the other lever, the traceability requirement in the IT Rules 2021, which demands identification of a message's "first originator". WhatsApp challenged it in the Delhi High Court as incompatible with encryption.
- Argument: remedies built for feeds either do nothing in encrypted apps or require breaking encryption, which trades one democratic good (privacy, safe dissent) for another (information integrity). This is why one verdict cannot cover both architectures.

**V. Counterargument and rebuttal (about 250 words)**
- Counterargument, stated fairly in two parts. First, the distinction is collapsing: large groups, Channels and cross-posting from public platforms make WhatsApp look more like a broadcaster. Second, Banaji & Bhat show the violence followed existing caste, religious and class prejudice, so blaming design misplaces the cause.
- Rebuttal to the first: the blurring is a matter of degree. Wherever content is encrypted and passed on through personal trust, the levers available still differ.
- Rebuttal to the second: concede it, and use it. The mechanism framing explains which pre-existing vulnerabilities each design activates, and why private-messaging harms need offline remedies such as policing, local institutions and media literacy, rather than platform fixes alone.

**VI. Conclusion (about 150 words)**
- Restate: the useful question is which mechanism, which harm and which lever.
- Implication for policy: regulate feeds through ranking transparency and audit. Treat encrypted messaging through friction plus state and civic capacity, not by weakening encryption.
- Close by returning to Rainpada: a design change came after the deaths, and the forwarding cap alone could not have prevented them.

## Sources

- Banaji, S. and Bhat, R. (2019). *WhatsApp Vigilantes: An Exploration of Citizen Reception and Circulation of WhatsApp Misinformation Linked to Mob Violence in India.* London School of Economics, Department of Media and Communications.
- Garimella, K. and Eckles, D. (2020). "Images and Misinformation in Political Groups: Evidence from WhatsApp in India." *Harvard Kennedy School Misinformation Review* 1(5).
- Guess, A. et al. (2023). "How Do Social Media Feed Algorithms Affect Attitudes and Behavior in an Election Campaign?" *Science* 381(6656).
- Huszár, F. et al. (2022). "Algorithmic Amplification of Politics on Twitter." *PNAS* 119(1).
- Melo, P. et al. (2019). "Can WhatsApp Counter Misinformation by Limiting Message Forwarding?" *Complex Networks 2019* (preprint on arXiv).

# Thesis

**Working thesis:**
Asking whether social media is "good" or "bad" for democracy is a category error, because democratic effects follow from specific architectural features rather than from "social media" as a whole. India's WhatsApp lynchings of 2017–18 show that harm arose from one particular combination: encrypted private messaging, frictionless one-tap forwarding, and closed groups of trusted contacts. Together these made rumours both highly persuasive and impossible to hold anyone accountable for. WhatsApp's July 2018 forwarding limit shows that the democratically preferable response is to add friction by design, rather than to restrict content or let the state trace message originators. Design friction slows harmful virality without giving the state a surveillance tool. However, it treats the speed of spread, not the underlying prejudice, so it is necessary but not sufficient.

**Shorter version, if you want something punchier:**
The democratic impact of social media depends on its architecture, and India's WhatsApp lynchings show that slowing how messages move is a better democratic remedy than policing what they say or tracing who said them.

---

# Outline (≈1,500 words)

## I. Introduction (~175 words)

**Hook:** On 1 July 2018 in Rainpada, Dhule district, Maharashtra, a mob killed five men after WhatsApp rumours warned of child kidnappers in the area. This was one of dozens of similar killings across India in 2017–18 (e.g., Karbi Anglong, Assam, June 2018; Bidar, Karnataka, July 2018).

**Move:** Most debate asks whether platforms like this are good or bad for democracy. That framing hides the more useful question: *which design features* produce which democratic effects?

**Thesis:** As above.

**Roadmap:** (1) a framework for treating design as regulation; (2) how WhatsApp's architecture turned rumour into violence; (3) why the forwarding limit beats the alternatives; (4) the strongest objection, that prejudice rather than design is the real cause.

## II. Framework: Architecture as Regulation (~200 words)

**Topic sentence:** To see why the good-or-bad framing fails, we need to treat platform design as a form of governance in its own right.

**Evidence and points:**
- **Lessig, *Code and Other Laws of Cyberspace* (1999)/*Code 2.0* (2006):** behaviour is regulated by four forces: law, norms, markets, and architecture ("code is law"). The forwarding limit is a clear case of regulation through architecture.
- **Distinguish two models of communication:**
  - *Public algorithmic feeds* (Facebook News Feed, X, YouTube): content is visible, so it can be moderated, fact-checked, and studied, but algorithms amplify it.
  - *Private encrypted messaging* (WhatsApp): content is invisible to the platform, so it cannot be moderated. It spreads through personal trust networks, not algorithms.
- **Key claim:** These two models produce different risks and therefore need different remedies. You can't moderate content you can't see, so with WhatsApp the only available lever is design.

## III. How WhatsApp's Architecture Produced the Lynchings (~325 words)

**Topic sentence:** The lynchings were not simply "misinformation online." They resulted from three design features that, combined, made rumours credible, fast, and untraceable.

**Feature 1: Trusted, closed networks.**
- Messages arrive from family, caste, village, and neighbourhood groups, not from strangers. Trust in the sender carries over to the content.
- **Evidence:** Banaji & Bhat, *WhatsApp Vigilantes* (LSE, 2019): users trusted messages from people they knew and from ideologically aligned groups.
- **Optional additional evidence:** the BBC World Service study *Duty, Identity, Credibility* (Chakrabarti et al., 2018).

**Feature 2: Frictionless forwarding that strips context.**
- Before July 2018, a forwarded message looked the same as an original one. There was a quick-forward button beside media, and a message could go to up to 256 chats at once.
- Images and videos, often old or from other countries, travelled without any source information.
- **Evidence:** Garimella & Eckles, "Images and Misinformation in Political Groups: Evidence from WhatsApp in India," *HKS Misinformation Review* (2020): image-based misinformation was widespread in public political groups.

**Feature 3: Encryption makes content invisible.**
- End-to-end encryption means neither WhatsApp nor fact-checkers can see what is spreading until offline violence reveals it.

**Analytical point:** None of these features is harmful on its own. Encryption protects dissidents and journalists, and trusted networks support everyday civic life. *The harm came from their combination.* This is why "good vs. bad" is the wrong question.

## IV. Three Possible Responses, and Why Friction Wins (~375 words)

**Topic sentence:** The Indian case offered three possible responses (content removal, traceability, and design friction), and only friction addresses the harm without damaging democratic values.

**Option A: Content moderation/takedowns.**
- This is impossible on an encrypted platform without breaking encryption.
- The state's fallback has been internet shutdowns. India leads the world in shutdowns (Access Now's annual #KeepItOn reports). Shutdowns are a blunt tool that silence everyone, including people trying to debunk rumours.

**Option B: Traceability.**
- In July 2018, the Ministry of Electronics and IT pressed WhatsApp to act. Later, Rule 4(2) of the IT Rules, 2021 required large messaging platforms to identify the "first originator" of messages.
- WhatsApp challenged this in the Delhi High Court in 2021.
- **Argument:** Traceability gives the state a tool that would also expose government critics. In a context of democratic backsliding, this is a serious cost. It also targets the person who *created* a rumour, when the harm actually comes from thousands of people *forwarding* it.

**Option C: Design friction (WhatsApp's actual response).**
- July 2018: forwarding was limited to five chats in India, the quick-forward button beside media was removed, and a "Forwarded" label was introduced.
- January 2019: the five-chat limit was extended globally.
- April 2020: "highly forwarded" messages were limited to one chat at a time. WhatsApp reported a 70% drop in such messages.
- **Argument:** These changes are *content-neutral*. They apply to all messages equally, they don't require anyone to read messages, and they don't require identifying users. The "Forwarded" label restores some of the context that forwarding strips away.

**Concluding sentence for the section:** Friction is the only option that respects both free expression and privacy, which makes it the most democratically legitimate option.

## V. Counterargument and Rebuttal (~275 words)

**Counterargument 1 (the strongest): the cause is prejudice, not design.**
- Banaji & Bhat argue that misinformation spread because it confirmed existing communal, caste, and anti-outsider prejudices. Victims were often outsiders, migrants, or members of minority groups. On this view, focusing on design lets political actors off the hook.
- **Rebuttal:** Concede the core point. Design doesn't create prejudice. But design determines how *fast* prejudice can mobilise a crowd and how *far* it reaches. A rumour that takes days to spread gives police and local fact-checkers time to respond. This is why the thesis claims "necessary but not sufficient."
- **Supporting detail:** Offline interventions mattered too. Examples include the Supreme Court's guidelines in *Tehseen S. Poonawalla v. Union of India* (17 July 2018) and police awareness campaigns in Telangana's Jogulamba Gadwal district.

**Counterargument 2: friction doesn't actually work.**
- de Freitas Melo et al., "Can WhatsApp Counter Misinformation by Limiting Message Forwarding?" (Complex Networks, 2019): forwarding limits delay the spread of content but don't stop highly viral content from eventually reaching large audiences.
- **Rebuttal:** For lynchings, delay is exactly what matters. Violence happens within a short window of panic, so slowing the spread directly reduces the danger.

**Optional counterargument 3:** It is undemocratic for a private company, rather than an elected parliament, to make these decisions. You could briefly concede this, then argue that design standards could be *mandated* by law, which is a better role for the state than traceability.

## VI. Conclusion (~150 words)

- **Restate the thesis in new language:** The lynchings were a design problem amplifying a social problem.
- **Broaden the point:** The same analysis applies elsewhere. Researchers have studied WhatsApp misinformation during Brazil's 2018 election (Resende et al., 2019). Telegram has similar affordances. Public feeds need different remedies, such as changes to algorithmic ranking.
- **Final line:** Democracies should stop asking whether social media is good or bad, and start asking which design features they are willing to require.

---

# Recommended Sources (core five; you need three)

1. **Banaji, S. & Bhat, R. (2019).** *WhatsApp Vigilantes: An Exploration of Citizen Reception and Circulation of WhatsApp Misinformation Linked to Mob Violence in India.* LSE Department of Media and Communications. *Your most important empirical source, and also the strongest counterargument.*
2. **Lessig, L. (2006).** *Code: Version 2.0.* Basic Books. *Provides the theoretical framework.*
3. **Garimella, K. & Eckles, D. (2020).** "Images and Misinformation in Political Groups: Evidence from WhatsApp in India." *Harvard Kennedy School Misinformation Review.*
4. **de Freitas Melo, P., Vieira, C. C., Garimella, K., Vaz de Melo, P. O. S., & Benevenuto, F. (2019).** "Can WhatsApp Counter Misinformation by Limiting Message Forwarding?" *Complex Networks 2019.*
5. **Arun, C. (2019).** "On WhatsApp, Rumours, Lynchings, and the Indian Government." *Economic & Political Weekly*, 54(6). *Useful for the state-response and traceability section.*

**Primary sources:** WhatsApp blog posts announcing the forwarding changes (July 2018, January 2019, April 2020); the IT Rules 2021, Rule 4(2); *Tehseen S. Poonawalla v. Union of India* (2018).

## Thesis

Social media has been good for democracy as participation and bad for it as governance. By making it dramatically easier for citizens to find one another and mobilize, it has expanded participatory democracy. But by bypassing linkage institutions and removing the friction Madison built into the extended republic, it has weakened the parties, organized groups and deliberation that turn public energy into durable policy and peaceful compromise.

## Outline (about 1,500 words)

**I. Introduction (about 175 words)**
- **Opening:** Social media is usually judged by what it lets people *do*, such as protest, post and organize. Democracy also has to *decide* and *govern*. Judging the platforms by mobilization alone captures only half the picture.
- **Definition of democracy:** Keep it broad, as you asked, and define it explicitly. One option from the AP Government curriculum is the three models:
  - Participatory democracy: broad citizen involvement.
  - Pluralist democracy: organized groups competing for influence.
  - Elite democracy: limited participation, with decisions filtered through representatives and institutions.
  - State that the essay judges social media against all three.
- **Thesis.**
- **Roadmap:** Three familiar cases, each reread to separate mobilization from governance.

**II. The participatory gain is real (about 225 words)**
- Social media lowers the cost of political action. Citizens can find like-minded people, coordinate quickly and reach a mass audience without money or institutional backing.
- By the participatory model's standard, this is a clear democratic good. More people can enter politics, and faster.
- **Federalist No. 10 link:** Madison argued that a large republic would make it harder for people with a shared grievance to "discover their own strength" and "act in unison." Social media removes that barrier almost entirely.
- **Pivot:** Whether that is good or bad depends on what happens *after* people mobilize. The three cases test that.

**III. Case 1: Egypt, 2011, reread (about 275 words)**
- **Standard reading:** The "Facebook revolution" shows social media empowering citizens against a dictator. Mubarak fell after eighteen days of protest.
- **Against the grain:** The networked youth movement that filled Tahrir Square did not win the elections that followed. The Muslim Brotherhood won the 2012 presidency. It had spent decades building offline organization, and the youth movement had not. The military removed President Morsi in 2013.
- **Mechanism:** Speed of mobilization stood in for organizational capacity. A movement that can gather a million people in days has not necessarily built the structures that negotiate, field candidates or govern.
- **Point for the thesis:** This is participatory success alongside a failure in what the pluralist model requires, which is organized, durable groups.

**IV. Case 2: The 2016 US election and Cambridge Analytica, reread (about 275 words)**
- **Standard reading:** Data-driven micro-targeting manipulated voters.
- **Against the grain:** The evidence that psychographic targeting changed votes is weak. The UK Information Commissioner's 2020 investigation found Cambridge Analytica's methods were largely standard and less powerful than the firm advertised. The deeper story is structural. Social media let candidates reach voters directly and build movements outside party control.
- **Mechanism:** Parties are *linkage institutions*, and one of their jobs is to screen candidates and build coalitions. Direct-to-voter platforms weaken that gatekeeping role.
- **Balance:** This cuts both ways. Weaker gatekeeping opens politics to outsiders, which is a participatory good. It also removes a filter that elite and pluralist models depend on.
- **Point for the thesis:** The harm is not mind control. It is that social media hollows out an institution that helps the system govern.

**V. Case 3: The 2020 racial justice protests, reread (about 250 words)**
- **Standard reading:** Social media spread video of George Floyd's killing and produced one of the largest protest movements in US history.
- **Against the grain:** The mobilization was enormous, but the federal legislative result was limited. The George Floyd Justice in Policing Act passed the House in 2021. Bipartisan Senate negotiations then collapsed, and no federal bill became law.
- **Mechanism:** Turning public pressure into a statute requires sustained interest-group work, coalition building and compromise in Congress. Those slow processes are the ones viral mobilization tends to skip.
- **Fairness:** Acknowledge real state and local policy changes, and note that the Senate's own rules mattered. This keeps the claim measured.

**VI. Counterargument and response (about 175 words)**
- **Counterargument:** Each failure has non-digital causes, including military power in Egypt, polarization in the US and the filibuster in the Senate. Social media is being blamed for problems it did not create.
- **Response:** Grant the point partly. Then narrow the claim: social media did not create these obstacles, but it shifted citizens' energy toward fast mobilization and away from building the organizations needed to overcome them.
- **Contrast:** The civil rights movement of the 1950s and 1960s relied on churches, the NAACP and years of slow organizing. It produced the Civil Rights Act of 1964.

**VII. Conclusion (about 125 words)**
- **Restate the thesis:** Social media is good for the first step of democracy and weak at the steps that follow.
- **Return to the definition:** Social media raises participatory democracy but weakens the pluralist and elite structures that translate participation into policy.
- **Closing line:** The question for American democracy is whether citizens can rebuild the organizations that social media lets them skip, not whether they can make their voices heard.

## Thesis

Social media has been good for democracy's voice but bad for its machinery. It lets ordinary people unite and challenge power faster than ever, as the Arab Spring showed, but it does little to build the parties, compromises and trusted institutions that turn protest into lasting self-government. Its effect on any democracy depends on whether those institutions are strong enough to channel the energy it creates.

## Outline (about 1,500 words)

**I. Introduction (~175 words)**
- **Hook:** Egypt, 2011. Protests organized partly through Facebook and Twitter forced Hosni Mubarak out in 18 days. Two years later, the military removed Egypt's first freely elected president, and the country was back under military rule.
- **Question:** If social media could topple a dictator, why couldn't it help build a democracy?
- **Thesis.**
- **Roadmap:** first voice, then machinery, then what decides which one wins.

**II. Framework: what democracy needs (~200 words)**
- **Voice:** people can speak, organize, protest and hold leaders accountable.
- **Machinery:** linkage institutions such as parties, interest groups, elections and the press turn opinions into policy and let opponents compromise.
- **Federalist 10:** Madison argued that a large republic makes it hard for a faction to "discover their own strength" and "act in unison."
- **Key move:** Social media removes the distance that slowed factions down. That helps a majority facing a dictator, and it is risky inside a working democracy.

**III. Good for voice (~325 words)**
- **Arab Spring:** Tunisia and Egypt in 2011. Online networks let people see that others shared their anger, coordinate protests and get images past state media.
- **Why this matters:** It lowered the cost of participation for people with no party or organization behind them.
- **Concede fully:** This is a real democratic gain and should be treated as one.

**IV. Bad for machinery (~400 words)**
- **Egypt after Mubarak:** The movement grew fast but had few leaders, little organization and no shared plan. Better-organized groups, the Muslim Brotherhood and then the military, filled the gap. Sociologist Zeynep Tufekci (*Twitter and Tear Gas*) argues that easy online organizing skips the slow work that builds staying power.
- **India and Myanmar:** Speed without checks. WhatsApp rumors in India were linked to mob killings in 2017–18, and a 2018 UN fact-finding report said Facebook played a "determining role" in spreading hate against the Rohingya. In both cases, information moved faster than any institution could respond.
- **Connect to the frame:** Each case shows voice growing faster than the machinery meant to channel it.

**V. Counterargument and response (~225 words)**
- **Counterargument:** Armies and economics caused these failures, not social media.
- **Response:** Social media didn't cause the failures, but it shaped the kind of movement that formed: fast, broad and loosely organized, which made it easier to defeat.
- **Taiwan:** The vTaiwan project used online tools to help citizens and officials reach agreement on issues like Uber regulation. That shows the tools can strengthen machinery when they are designed and used for it.

**VI. Conclusion (~175 words)**
- **Restate:** Social media amplifies voice, and institutions decide what that voice becomes.
- **Return to the hook:** Egypt had the voice in 2011 but lacked the machinery to keep what it won.
- **Takeaway for an AP Gov reader:** Democracies that keep strong linkage institutions can absorb social media's energy, and weak ones get overwhelmed by it.

# Tidemark: a basement flood alarm that won't let a building sleep through it

## The idea
In December 2023 your apartment basement flooded and around 30 cars were damaged, because nobody noticed the water rising overnight. Tidemark is a sensor and server that watches basement water level continuously. It works out how fast the water is rising and when it will reach tyre height. It alerts residents early, then escalates from a group message to a phone call to the next person on the list, until someone confirms they're on it.

The engineering that technical judges can probe:

1. **Rate, not threshold.** A fixed "water detected" trigger fires too late. Tidemark fits a slope to the last N readings and projects the time until the car line is reached.
2. **Silence is a failure, not an all-clear.** If the sensor stops reporting, that gets alerted too. A dead sensor at 3am is the same failure as nobody watching.
3. **Escalation with acknowledgement.** An alert isn't "sent" until a person confirms it.

## What you'd build

**Hardware (your hardware teammate)**
- Two water-level sensors at different heights in a clear container, with the "floor" and "tyre line" marked on the side. Two sensors give redundancy and a plausibility cross-check: if the upper one reads wet and the lower one dry, it's a fault, not a flood.
- The Arduino streams JSON lines over USB serial at 2 Hz, for example `{"s1": 512, "s2": 0, "t": 18234}`. The laptop acts as the building gateway. That's simpler and more reliable on demo day than Wi-Fi.
- Calibration: dip each sensor to 4 or 5 depths measured with a ruler and record the raw values. The backend interpolates between those points, because cheap resistive sensors aren't linear.

**Backend (you, Python)**
- **Serial reader → smoother → estimator.** Use an exponential moving average on raw readings, then linear regression over a sliding window to get the slope in cm/min. Compute an ETA to the car line only when the slope is clearly positive and the fit is decent. This keeps sensor jitter from setting off false alarms.
- **State machine:** `NORMAL → RISING → ALERT → ACKNOWLEDGED`, plus `SENSOR_FAULT` (no reading for X seconds, or the two sensors disagree).
- **Escalation ladder:**
  1. A Telegram group message with an "I'm on it" inline button.
  2. No acknowledgement within the timeout triggers a Twilio voice call that asks the person to press 1 to confirm.
  3. No answer moves the call to the next person on the list.
- **FastAPI plus a WebSocket** pushes live state to the dashboard. SQLite logs every reading and event.
- **Replay mode:** record one real pour as a CSV on Saturday. Replaying it through the same pipeline gives you repeatable tests and a fallback if the hardware fails on stage.
- **Demo scaling:** make thresholds and timeouts config values, so the jar's 15 cm and a 3-minute pitch stand in for a real basement and a real night. Tell the judges this openly.

**Dashboard and alerts (your designer)**
- One screen with:
  - a large water-level gauge with the tyre line drawn on it
  - the current rise rate and a countdown such as "reaches cars in 1:40"
  - the escalation timeline, showing who was messaged, who was called, and who acknowledged
  - a sensor-health light
- **Alert wording for someone woken at night:** short, specific, and actionable. For example: "Basement water rising 2 cm/min. Reaches car level in about 12 min. Move cars now. Tap if you're handling it."
- **A QR card** that adds judges to the Telegram alert group.

## 36-hour plan

| Hours | Hardware | Backend (you) | Design |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0–6 | Wire both sensors, serial output, first calibration | Serial reader, smoothing, slope and ETA; **run the pour test** | Dashboard layout, alert wording |
| 6–18 | Mount sensors in the container, mark lines, repeat pours | State machine, Telegram bot with ack button, WebSocket | Build the dashboard against fake data |
| 18–30 | Make it robust: secure the wiring, dry the sensors between runs | Twilio call with keypress ack, fault detection, replay mode, SQLite log | Connect to the live feed, QR card, one architecture slide |
| 30–36 | **Feature freeze.** Full rehearsals with real water | Tune thresholds for the jar | Rehearse, record a backup video |

**If you fall behind,** cut in this order: the second sensor, then the Twilio call (keep Telegram), then the database log. Never cut fault detection. It's your strongest technical moment.

## 3-minute demo

Skip the problem slide. The water is the problem slide.

- **0:00–0:20.** The container is on the table and the dashboard is on screen. One person speaks: "In December 2023 our apartment basement flooded. About 30 cars were damaged, because nobody noticed the water rising overnight. We built the thing that would have noticed."
- **0:20–0:40.** "Scan this to join our building's alert group." The judges scan the QR card.
- **0:40–1:20.** Start pouring slowly. The gauge rises, the rate appears, and the countdown to the tyre line starts. "Notice it's predicting *when*, not just reporting *that*."
- **1:20–1:40.** The alert fires while the water is still well below the line, and the judges' phones buzz. Nobody taps "I'm on it."
- **1:40–2:10.** The timeout expires and the phone on the table rings. A teammate answers and presses 1. The dashboard's escalation timeline flips to "Acknowledged" with the time and the teammate's name.
- **2:10–2:40.** The judge-bait moment. Unplug the sensor. Within seconds: "SENSOR OFFLINE. Basement unmonitored." "A silent sensor is the same failure as nobody watching, so we treat it as an emergency."
- **2:40–3:00.** Show the architecture slide (sensor → gateway → estimator → escalation) and close: "That night, the water rose with nobody watching. Tidemark would have woken someone while there was still time to move the cars."

**Stage safety:** run the dashboard on localhost so venue Wi-Fi only matters for the alerts. Have the replay CSV loaded behind a single keypress in case the hardware fails. Keep a towel and a tray under the container.

# Wakeline: a basement flood alarm that won't let everyone sleep through it

## The idea

In December 2023 our apartment basement flooded overnight. Around 30 cars were damaged, and nobody noticed the water rising after midnight.

Detecting the water wasn't the hard part. A wet sensor costs a few dollars. The hard part is that at 1am the water rises in an empty room while everyone who could act is asleep upstairs. A beeping alarm in the basement reaches no one, and a single push notification is easy to sleep through.

Wakeline handles the gap between detection and action. It does three things.

1. **Measures how fast the water is rising**, not just whether it is there.
2. **Turns that rate into a deadline:** the minutes left until water reaches the height where car damage starts.
3. **Escalates until a human acknowledges it.** It calls a phone, waits, then calls the next person and the next, getting more urgent as the deadline gets closer.

The climate link is direct. Heavier downpours are a well-documented effect of warming, and underground parking is where that water collects. This is adaptation for a building that has already flooded once.

## What we'd build

**Hardware (your hardware person)**
- Mount the water-level sensors at several fixed heights on a vertical stick inside the "basement." The heights could be floor level, a few centimetres up, and your car-damage threshold. Discrete heights are more robust than one cheap analog strip. Each sensor that trips gives a clean timestamp, and the time between trips gives you the rate.
- The Arduino reads the sensors and streams JSON lines over USB serial. If your board has Wi-Fi, it can post over HTTP instead, but serial removes venue Wi-Fi from the hardware path.
- Add a local buzzer and LED on the Arduino as a last-resort alarm if the network dies.

**Backend (Python)**
- **Ingest:** A serial reader using `pyserial` debounces readings. A sensor must stay wet for a few consecutive reads before it counts, so a splash doesn't trigger a 1am call.
- **Rate and deadline:** For each pair of trip events, compute rate = Δheight / Δtime, then deadline = (threshold height − current height) / rate. Severity is set by the deadline, not the level. Water at 2 cm rising fast is more urgent than water at 4 cm sitting still.
- **Escalation engine:** A small state machine.
  - Tier 1 calls the on-duty resident.
  - If no one presses 1 within N minutes, Tier 2 calls the building manager and texts everyone with a car on that level.
  - When the deadline drops below a set number of minutes, everyone gets called at once.
  - Use Twilio for voice and SMS. A voice call with "press 1 to acknowledge" is the core of the product, because ringing is what wakes people. Every event and acknowledgement is logged with a timestamp.
- **API:** A FastAPI app that serves the live state to the screen.

**Screen (your designer)**
- One page with three parts: the water height on a live line, a large countdown ("Water reaches car level in 11 min"), and the escalation ladder showing who has been called, who answered, and who is next.
- Design for the person half-awake on their phone at 1am, not for a judge.

**Stretch, only if Sunday morning is free**
- Pull a rainfall forecast from Open-Meteo (free, no key) to put the system on high alert on heavy-rain nights: lower thresholds and a heads-up text at bedtime.

### 36-hour split
- **First 12 hours:** Hardware gets sensors reading reliably over serial. Backend builds the rate and deadline logic against fake serial data. The designer builds the screen against a mocked API.
- **Next 12 hours:** Connect the real sensors, add Twilio calls and the escalation timer, and run the first full pour test.
- **Last 12 hours:** Tune debounce and thresholds by pouring water repeatedly. Build the demo rig, run the demo five times, and fix whatever breaks. Freeze features well before judging.

## Demo plan: replay the night

The demo is your flood, replayed at table scale, with the beats keyed to water height instead of a slide deck.

**The rig:** a clear plastic tub as the basement, the sensor stick at one end, and a row of toy cars on the floor. Mark a line on the side at "car damage." Use a jug of water, or a small pump if your hardware person wants a steady, repeatable rise. The laptop screen is mirrored to the projector, and one team member's phone is face-up on the table with the volume on.

1. **The setup (one sentence):** "December 2023, our basement flooded overnight and damaged around 30 cars because nobody noticed the water rising after midnight. This is that basement, and it's now 1am."
2. **The water starts:** Pour slowly. The first sensor trips and the screen shows water detected, with the rate still being calculated. Nothing rings yet. Point out that a splash wouldn't have triggered this, because of the debounce.
3. **The rate appears:** The second sensor trips. The deadline locks in ("car level in N minutes") and the phone on the table rings out loud. Let it ring and don't answer. That is the 1am scenario.
4. **The escalation:** After the timeout, the ladder moves. A second phone rings and the texts go out. Pour faster, and the room watches the deadline shrink and the severity jump.
5. **The acknowledgement:** A teammate answers and presses 1. The ladder shows who acknowledged it and when. Say what would happen next in the building: someone goes down and moves the cars.
6. **The technical point (30 seconds):** Show the rate-to-deadline calculation and the escalation state machine on one slide. That is the hard part, and it's why this isn't just a leak beeper.

**Make it survive the room**
- Set demo timeouts to about 20 seconds, so escalation happens on stage instead of after a 10-minute wait.
- If Twilio or the Wi-Fi fails, the Arduino buzzer and LED still fire and the screen still shows the ladder. Say so out loud, because that fallback is a real feature.
- Pre-wet nothing. Dry the sensors with a cloth between runs, and practise the pour speed so the deadline lands in a believable range.
